secrets-webhooks-07 medium to lowStripe Restricted Keys for narrow contexts is correct practice, but its own rule text concedes there is no such narrow context today: every current Stripe path creates charges, manages payouts, or handles Connect. A least-privilege rule with zero call sites to apply to is a note for the first read-only reporting job, not a principle to adopt now.
authz-rls-01 critical to not a live hole; re-file as the migration-versus-live principleAlready corrected by the orchestrator's own live query. pg_policies on public.reviews returns exactly four correctly-scoped policies and the permissive USING(true) UPDATE policy does not exist live; across all 150 public tables there are zero bare true write policies and RLS is enabled on 150 of 150. The migration-file half is true, which is why this belongs in merge group C rather than in the critical bucket. Same correction applies to data-money-03, whose fabricated amenity booleans are all false in the live table (0 true across 20 active salons).
mergeOne principle wearing several hats
api-contracts-03, ethics-psychology-02, trust-01-phone-verification-silent-noop, trust-03-account-warnings-write-only, observability-1, copy-i18n-08, motion-04, testing-release-01, testing-release-03, secrets-webhooks-09THE SILENT NO-OP RULE APPLIES TO THE MACHINERY, NOT ONLY TO PRODUCT FILTERS. The project's pinned rule already says: prove behavior, not existence; a filter must DISCRIMINATE, not merely render or return 200. Extend that same proof obligation, unchanged in wording, to every other thing in this estate that can look wired and do nothing: a consent or preference toggle must have a proven reader on a real send path; a verification endpoint that returns verified:true must persist the fact in the same request (and the column it writes must exist in the live schema); a table that records a penalty must have a reader that applies the consequence; a cron-health check must distinguish 'ran and failed' from 'never ran'; a gate, lint script or npm check must be proven to fire on a crafted failing input, not merely to exist in package.json; a CI job that can skip its whole body and still report green is a placebo; and every Terms of Service promise about verification, enforcement or consequence needs one end-to-end test that exercises it. One rule, one existing name, one new sentence about scope.
testing-release-01, testing-release-02, testing-release-10, accessibility-09, layout-geometry-06, performance-01, performance-02, secrets-webhooks-02, secrets-webhooks-06, color-tokens-01, color-tokens-05, copy-i18n-01, copy-i18n-04, copy-i18n-07, fe-01, fe-04NOTHING MAY BE PRESCRIBED INTO CI UNTIL CI EXISTS ON THE REMOTE DEFAULT BRANCH. Verified this session: origin/main is at 4dd8bc15f (2026-05-21), local main is 1,604 commits ahead, and the GitHub repo's .github/workflows contains exactly one file (cron-jobs.yml); gh run list --workflow=quality.yml returns 404, not found on the default branch, and the five most recent runs of the one deployed workflow all failed in 5 to 7 seconds. Sixteen findings here propose a new CI job (a11y lint, axe target-size, Lighthouse budgets, npm audit ratchet, gitleaks, select(*) ratchet, i18n key parity, jscpd, diff-scoped lint). Every one of them is downstream of a single prerequisite, and adopting them as law before that prerequisite is met writes sixteen false guarantees into the doctrine. The merged principle: any doc sentence claiming a CI guarantee must name the workflow file AND its last green run on the remote default branch, and a health check must assert that the local workflow set equals the remote workflow set. Fix the prerequisite (push, add the missing secrets, confirm one green run), then reconsider the sixteen, most of which will still not be worth their maintenance at 28 salons.
authz-rls-01, authz-rls-06, authz-rls-09, data-money-03, data-money-07THE MIGRATIONS FOLDER IS A HISTORY, NOT A DESCRIPTION OF THE DATABASE, AND THE DIVERGENCE IS THE RISK. Two independent agents in this run reported a CRITICAL that was a migration-file truth presented as a live truth (a permissive reviews UPDATE policy that does not exist live, and hash-fabricated amenity booleans that are false for all 20 active salons). Every claim about current schema, policy or data is made against the live database; the migration folder is evidence only about what a REPLAY would produce. Both questions are legitimate and they are different: 'is this true now' and 'would a restore make this true'. Every audit states which one it answered. The corollary is the actual danger and it subsumes the restore-drill finding: a replay-only landmine is invisible to every check this estate runs, because nothing ever replays the folder onto a clean database. One real restore drill closes both halves at once, so it outranks all four of the RLS-policy-hygiene findings it absorbs.
hierarchy-density-01, hierarchy-density-02, responsive-desktop-01, imagery-icons-05EVERY MEASURED DESIGN FLOOR IS ENFORCED AGAINST MOCKUPS AND NEVER AGAINST THE SHIPPED PAGE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM. Measured live this session at 390x844: /de home is 4.4% imagery against a 33% floor with 7 distinct font sizes against a ceiling of 4 and 42.1% of text at weight >= 600 against a 30% ceiling; /de/basel is 0.0% imagery, zero images of any kind on a 9,325px page, while 20 of 28 salons have a usable cover_photo_url in the database. Meanwhile mockup-floors-gate.py's entire check is the regex `floors:\s*\S.{20,}`, that is, the presence of twenty characters after the word 'floors:'. The merged rule replaces four separate proposals (measure the gate instead of grepping for a comment, add a Floors row to SENIOR_SCORECARD, extend the floors to desktop and tablet, reconcile the documented fallback with the shipped component): run check-geometry.mjs --floors-only against the SHIPPED routes on real data as the acceptance condition, at every viewport the estate claims to support, and treat a mockup-only pass as no evidence. Nothing else on this list changes what a customer sees as directly.
api-contracts-10, authz-rls-04, data-money-01, observability-7, secrets-webhooks-08, privacy-compliance-01, performance-04, motion-07RESEARCH IS NOT LAW, AND THIS ESTATE IS PRODUCING RESEARCH FASTER THAN IT FREEZES DECISIONS. Eight findings across six domains say the same thing: _backend-system/ contains 15 research files and 8 audit files, its own README promises LAW.md, RATIONALE.md, AUDIT.md and QUESTIONS.md at the root, and none of those four exist. This is ONE work item (transcribe the existing Decision-candidates tables into one LAW.md, dated, one row per axis) and not eight principles. But it must be adopted together with law-layer-roi-test, because it is the exact shape that finding warns about: writing a sixteenth research topic (privacy) into a folder that has never frozen the first fifteen makes the problem worse, not better. Rule: a topic is done at 'law frozen and backlinked', never at 'research written', and no new research topic starts until the previous one has a LAW.md row.
gate-mute-forces-rescope, serial-gate-count-cap, hook-sprawl-ceiling, canonical-doc-size-ceiling, law-layer-roi-test, gate-retirement-policy, no-authoring-time-tier-check, doc-to-gate-drift-reconciliation, design-regression-not-fed-to-code-regression-system, memory-consolidation-no-triggerTHE LAW LAYER GETS A BUDGET AND A DECAY PATH, NOT TEN NEW META-RULES. Ten separate governance findings all describe one condition: the estate grows law faster than it retires it, and the excess is discharged through skip flags rather than through decisions. Measured: 164 hooks (134 global, 30 project), 410,091 words in _design-system top-level markdown, LOCKFILE at 19,637 words which the project CLAUDE.md itself says nobody re-reads before a small edit, 13+ PreToolUse gates denying one at a time on a single mockup Write, one 7-gate family skip-flagged 72 times in 6 days, 8 gates sitting on disk unwired while the law text cites one of them (no-decorative-image-gate.py) as if it were live. The single merged rule: every new law names the counted incidents from the last 90 days it would have prevented, its per-session cost, and the existing law it replaces; total wired hooks are capped with one-in-one-out past the current count; any gate skip-flagged more than 10 times in a rolling 7 days is auto-flagged for re-scope or retirement; and any law sentence that names a hook file is reconciled against the settings files by the health check. Adopting the other nine as separate rows would be the failure this rule exists to prevent.
accessibility-02, ia-navigation-02, typography-01ANYTHING RENDERED ABOVE THE [locale] SEGMENT MUST BE LOCALE-INDEPENDENT BY CONSTRUCTION. Verified live on /en/basel: document.documentElement.lang is 'de' on the English page (app/layout.tsx:39 hardcodes it, above the locale tree), and the skip link still reads 'Zum Inhalt springen'. app/not-found.tsx, the second one, hardcodes German 404 copy with a literal em dash next to the properly i18n'd app/[locale]/not-found.tsx. The root viewport export in the same file disables pinch-zoom for all four languages. One file, one structural rule, four defects: the root layout may contain no locale-dependent string and no user-hostile global (lang, skip link, viewport scalability); anything that must live there reads the locale from the request. A one-line CI grep for hardcoded German and lang= in app/layout.tsx is the check, once CI exists.
color-tokens-02, color-tokens-03, typography-02THE DESIGN SYSTEM'S REACH STOPS AT THE REACT TREE, AND THREE LIVE SURFACES ARE OUTSIDE IT. The salon payout invoice (app/api/salon/invoices/[payoutId]/route.ts, a document partners print), the transactional email templates (lib/email-templates/*.ts, still rendering pre-B&W-pivot teal #38B2AC and coral #FF6B6B), and lib/email.ts:584 (gift-card codes in font-family:monospace, a retired font by name) all generate their own HTML strings and therefore obey no token, no font law and no contrast check. One rule covers all three: any surface that emits HTML/CSS outside the component tree imports its colors, fonts and numerals from one shared exported constants file mirroring the LOCKFILE table, and the drift checker's scan globs include it. This is worth more than most of the visual findings because these are the only Solen artifacts a partner keeps a copy of.
orch-output-01, orch-output-02, orch-output-03, orch-output-05, orch-output-13, agent-output-1, agent-output-2, agent-output-3A REPORT STATES ITS NEGATIVE SPACE, ITS SAMPLE, AND ITS METHOD, OR IT IS A VIBE. Eight findings across two agents describe one discipline. Merged: every report that claims verification also names what was in scope and deliberately not checked; every claim derived from inspecting a set states how many of how many were inspected and how the sample was chosen ('12 of 357 route handlers across auth, booking and payments', never 'I checked the routes'); every number the assistant produced itself ships with the command that regenerates it and is rounded to the precision that method supports; hedges (should, presumably, likely, probably, I believe) are banned about anything runnable, readable or greppable, replaced by either the check or an explicit 'I did not check this'; and if the load-bearing claim of the turn could not be verified, that goes in the first line, above the work. This run is its own proof: three agents wrote 'every upload route trusts client file.type' having read four or five of them, and two wrote migration-file state as live state. Adopt this as ONE addition to REPORT_SYSTEM section 4, not as eight.
ia-navigation-01, ia-navigation-04, ia-navigation-05, states-forms-04IF THE USER CAN GET BACK TO IT, IT LIVES IN THE URL OR IN STORAGE, NEVER ONLY IN MEMORY. Four findings describe one boundary: the booking wizard holds all step state in React context with no popstate guard, /inspo seeds only two of six filter dimensions from searchParams while /search seeds all of them, no page restores scroll position on back-navigation, and multi-step forms lose everything on refresh. The merged rule is the state-ownership half of fe-03 applied to navigation: anything that should be shareable, back-button-safe, or survive a refresh (a filter, an active step, a search query, a selected date, a scroll position) lives in the URL or in per-flow session storage, and a flow that cannot be reconstructed from its URL alone must intercept back and refresh with the same confirmation its explicit exit control already shows. One rule replaces four surface-specific ones and also absorbs ia-navigation-10 (a query param name carries one meaning app-wide).

Judge 3, what the sweep could not see

20 net new
VerdictA 26-domain sweep can only find rules that are missing from a domain it was told exists, and it can only ever find them by proving a grep returns nothing. That shape has three consequences. First, it is additive by construction: 264 findings, and not one of them says an existing rule is wrong, too expensive, or should be deleted. For an estate whose owner's actual complaint is that rules get forgotten or outranked, a method that can only grow the law layer is pointed the wrong way. Second, nothing lives in the seams: no agent owned the conflict between an owner taste decision and a WCAG requirement, between the imagery floor and the LCP budget, or between what the ToS promises a customer and what it promises a salon, so each of those was found only as an instance inside one domain and never as the arbitration rule that is actually missing. Third, every agent audited the state the estate is in, and the estate has never been in the state that matters: pre-launch is treated as a permanent condition (there is a gate enforcing the pre-launch framing and no artifact anywhere naming what ends it), so the whole sweep is an audit of a rehearsal. The three largest things the sweep did not see are structural, not domain-shaped: there is exactly one Supabase project and the local .env.local carries its service-role key, so dev, seed scripts, kill-tests and production are the same live database; the precedence chain that resolves every conflict in this estate has no legal or safety tier at all; and a salon can be activated into the marketplace by an enforced code gate but has no defined way to leave it. My recommendation on the 264 stands separately from my own list: adopt the small verified-and-cheap subset now, and treat the rest as a backlog that must shrink before launch, not a list to be written into doctrine this month.
blind spotsWhy a 26-topic sweep misses these by construction
Cross-domain arbitration. No agent could propose the rule that resolves a conflict between two domains' floors, because such a rule belongs to neither domain.Each agent was scoped inside one named domain and asked what was missing from it. A conflict between the design imagery floor and the performance LCP budget appeared only as hierarchy-density-09, filed as a design gap. The WCAG-versus-owner-taste conflict appeared only as accessibility-01, filed as an a11y gap. In both cases the actual missing artifact is an arbitration rule that no domain owns.
The estate's relationship to time. Nobody audited the rule set against a state the product has never occupied.Agents compare current code to current law. Both are pre-launch. The rules that become wrong on the day of the first real booking (the prelaunch-reality-gate's whole discriminator, the no-real-customers memory entry, the pre-launch framing that makes every severity a conditional) are correct today, so no absence-proving grep can flag them.
The business as an artifact. What Solen promises each side, what it refuses to promise, and who wins when the two sides conflict.The domain list was technical and craft-shaped. The Terms of Service were read by exactly one agent, and only as a source of prose-versus-code mismatches (trust-01 to trust-06). Nobody was asked whether the promises themselves are the right ones, coherent with each other, or keepable by one person.
The owner as a component of the system: capacity, concurrent work, availability, and what happens when they are unreachable.No domain was called 'the human'. law-system-meta came closest with no-second-operator-onboarding-bound, but scoped it to a fresh agent's read time, not to the owner's own throughput. So 27 simultaneously ACTIVE workstreams and a scattered, undated owner-blocked backlog are invisible: they are not code and not law, they are load.
Endings and exits as lifecycle stages, rather than as defects inside an existing flow.An absence-proving agent finds a missing check inside a flow that exists. A flow that was never built at all produces no anchor to grep against. Salon offboarding has no route, no doc and no mention, so there was nothing for any domain agent to find missing from it.
Outcome measurement. Whether any of this made the product work.Every domain measures conformance of its own artifact: pixels against floors, routes against contracts, tokens against a palette. Nobody's domain was 'did a customer book'. The estate consequently has an extremely precise measurement culture pointed entirely at inputs.
Environment topology. Which database is production, which credentials exist where, and what a dev process may touch.This sits above application code and below infrastructure. Agents read app/, lib/, supabase/migrations/ and the law docs. The fact that .env.local is a symlink pointing every worktree at the production project ref, with the service-role key, is in none of those places.
Anything the estate itself has never named. The 26-domain taxonomy was derived from the estate being audited, so it inherits that estate's existing blind spots exactly.A sweep organised by the subject's own categories cannot discover a category the subject lacks. Design got seven domains; the business got one; the owner's own sustainability got a fraction of one; the customer's actual outcomes got none.
The wrongness of existing rules. The method can prove a rule is absent, never that a present rule is harmful, overpriced, or should be deleted.Each agent's evidence standard was a grep proving absence. There is no symmetric procedure for proving a rule costs more than it prevents, so the sweep's output is monotonically additive against an estate whose stated pain is rule volume and rules being outranked.
critical There is no staging: dev, seed scripts, kill-tests and production are one live databasejudge3-01
The rule to addName exactly one Supabase project as PRODUCTION and write its ref in a single place. No local dev process, seed script, kill-test, migration trial or agent session may hold that project's service-role key. Until a second project exists, every script that can write (seed, backfill, cleanup, kill-test, apply_migration) must read the configured project ref, compare it to the production ref, and refuse to run on a match unless the owner passes an explicit, per-invocation confirmation. Provisioning a second project is the real fix; the refusal check is what holds the line until then.
WhyThe whole estate's safety story assumes a boundary that does not exist. The local .env.local is a symlink shared by every worktree, it carries SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, and the only Supabase URL present in any env file is the same project ref the orchestrator queried live. Claude Code runs with defaultMode bypassPermissions. So a single wrong script in a dev session writes to the same 150-table database that will hold real bookings and real money, with RLS bypassed by the service role, and no dialog in the way. Every backend finding in this run assumes an attacker or a bug; this is the case where a routine local command is sufficient. It is also why the migration-replay landmines the orchestrator found (the amenity-fabrication migration, the reviews RLS policy) are more dangerous than they look: the only database a replay could ever land on is the live one.
Proof/Users/sulo/Documents/solen/.claude/worktrees/quirky-ellis-ef5559/.env.local is a symlink to /Users/sulo/Documents/solen/.env.local; it contains one SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE key and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://tocfnsmxmdxkrcmjzzdw.supabase.co, which is the same ref the orchestrator ran its live SELECTs against. grep across all .env* files returns exactly one supabase.co host. /Users/sulo/.claude/settings.json line 4 sets defaultMode to bypassPermissions.
Lives inA new ENVIRONMENTS row in the project CLAUDE.md design/ops contract, plus _rules/DB_SCHEMA.md section 1, plus _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md
Enforced byA production-ref-guard PreToolUse hook that denies any Bash command containing the production project ref or invoking a known write-script while no confirmation flag is fresh, and a runtime assert at the top of every script in scripts/ that touches Supabase. Both are cheap and testable against a fake ref before arming.
critical The precedence chain has no legal or safety tier, so a taste rejection silently outranks a statutory floorjudge3-02
The rule to addInsert one tier into the precedence chain, directly below the owner's live literal ask and above everything else: statutory and safety floors. Named members: WCAG 2.1 A and AA on published surfaces, Swiss nFADP and GDPR obligations, the Preisbekanntgabeverordnung price-display rules, and any representation already made in the shipped Terms of Service. When a taste decision, a LOCKFILE row or a gate would breach one of these, it is not applied and it is not silently resolved either way: the session stops, names the specific requirement, and offers the owner an option that satisfies both. The owner may still overrule, but the overrule is recorded as a knowing legal exception with a date, not as a design preference.
WhyThe chain in the project CLAUDE.md runs owner ask, gates, LOCKFILE, pinned blocks, TASTE_LOG, memory, global rules, checklists. The word legal appears in it only as a UI-copy exemption. The consequence has already happened and this sweep found it three separate times without naming the cause: focus outlines are removed unconditionally for every device because rings were rejected on taste three times (accessibility-01), pinch-zoom is disabled sitewide (accessibility-03, typography-01), and a grey authorized for informational text computes at 2.54:1 (accessibility-05). Each was filed as an accessibility gap. The actual defect is upstream: an aesthetic preference and a legal floor were fed into a chain that has no way to tell them apart, and aesthetics sat higher. Adding twenty a11y rules does not fix a chain that will outrank them again next time.

critical Nothing in the estate defines the end of pre-launch, or lists what becomes wrong on that dayjudge3-03
The rule to addMaintain one LAUNCH.md with two sections and nothing else. Section A: the binary conditions that must all be true before the first real customer booking is accepted, each either true or false, no partial credit. Section B: the flip list, every gate file, memory entry, doctrine sentence and product default that becomes wrong the moment we are live, each with its exact path and its post-launch value. Launch is executed by walking section B, not by an announcement. Until section A is complete, any claim that a fix can wait because we are pre-launch must name the section A item it is parked behind.
WhyPre-launch is currently a permanent, self-reinforcing frame with no exit. A Stop gate enforces the conditional framing of every bug (prelaunch-reality-gate.py: a pre-launch bug is a WOULD, never a DID), a memory entry restates it, and the only way out is a manual skip flag. That gate is right about the past failure it was built for, and it also means the cheapest correct answer to any severity question is 'we are not live yet', forever, with no counter and no deadline. The sharpest evidence that the estate knows how to do this properly is that it already does it for the other side of the marketplace: POST /api/salon/go-live refuses to activate a salon without Stripe onboarding complete, a cover photo, at least one active service and prior admin approval. A salon has an enforced readiness gate. The platform has none.

WhyThis estate measures its inputs to three significant figures and its outputs not at all. The consequence is not just that nobody knows if the design law works. It is that the design law cannot be wrong: with no outcome number, a floor can only ever be complied with or violated, never disproved, which is exactly how an estate accumulates 410,000 words of unfalsifiable craft law. One number per feature is also the only cheap defence against that, and it costs a cell in a table.

high One-way doors and two-way doors get the same ceremony, so the cheap decisions are over-locked and the irreversible ones went in unremarkedjudge3-07
The rule to addClassify a decision before locking it. A one-way door is anything a customer, a salon, a payment processor or a search engine can come to rely on: a money representation, a schema shape, a public URL, a Terms of Service sentence, a payout policy. It requires a written rationale, a stated migration story for changing it later, and an explicit owner sign-off. A two-way door is anything reversible in an afternoon: a shadow value, a radius, a copy string, an animation curve. It gets decided fast, marked cheap-to-reverse, and is never allowed to consume a locking ceremony. Every LOCKFILE row and TASTE_LOG entry states which kind it is.
WhyThe estate applies maximum ceremony uniformly, and the result is inverted. Reversible aesthetics are frozen with dated owner stamps and defended by gates, while genuine one-way doors slipped in with no ceremony at all: two money representations coexist in the live schema with no law choosing one (integer Rappen in the booking path, numeric(10,2) in the retail-era tables), no law governs what happens when a salon's public slug would change (ia-navigation-06), and the shipped Terms of Service made at least three enforceable promises with no code behind them (trust-01, trust-02, trust-03). The cost of over-locking a two-way door is velocity. The cost of under-locking a one-way door is a migration you cannot perform because customers are standing on it.
ProofOrchestrator live verification section 3: bookings.paid_amount, platform_fee and net_amount are integer Rappen while retail-era migrations carry net_amount numeric(10,2), with no law choosing. Digest: ia-navigation-06 (no slug-change law), trust-01/02/03 (ToS promises with no implementation). Contrast the ceremony given to reversible values in the project CLAUDE.md design contract table.

Enforced byAuthoring-time: the taste-log entry template requires the field. Additionally, a short one-way-door register listing the handful that exist (money unit, slug scheme, ToS clauses, payout timing, booking reference format) so a session can check membership in one read instead of inferring it.

The rule to addFor each money-touching event class (first real booking, first payment capture, first refund, first payout to a salon, first no-show fee, first chargeback, first deletion request), the owner is notified on each of the first ten occurrences and reconciles it by hand against Stripe and the database within 24 hours, writing down what matched. Automation of that class is trusted only after those ten. If an event class reaches ten with no discrepancies, say so and stop watching it.
WhyEvery payment, payout and refund path in this product has executed only against test data. The estate's response to that risk so far has been to add more static guarantees, which is the expensive answer, and the sweep's response is to propose more of them. The cheap answer for a one-person marketplace with no on-call rotation is to watch the first few by hand, which is what a small operator can actually do and what no domain agent proposed because none of them was thinking about the first ninety days. It is also the fastest way to discover the class of defect this estate is most prone to and cannot test for, the silent no-op: a strike table nobody reads, an SMS verification that persists nothing, a chargeback that never touches the booking. Each of those would be caught on its first real occurrence by a human comparing two screens, and by nothing else currently in the estate.

The rule to addFor each of the five operations that cannot wait, refund a booking, suspend a salon, put the site into a maintenance state, restore the database, and rotate a leaked key, the runbook carries a human-executable version: dashboard clicks, or one copy-paste command, no agent required. Each is walked once by the owner before launch and the walk is dated. If an operation has no human version, that fact is written down as a known dependency on the assistant, not left implicit.
WhyThis is the capability half of the continuity problem and it is distinct from having the credentials. OPS_RUNBOOK.md's restore procedure is six steps ending in npm run smoke; the monitoring section describes what a cron logs; the backup path is a Next.js route triggered by a GitHub Action. All of it assumes a working toolchain and, in practice, a session. If the assistant is unavailable, changed by a provider update, or simply wrong at the moment it matters, the owner is holding a product they can only operate through an intermediary. The estate has 164 hooks teaching an assistant how to behave and not one page teaching the owner how to act alone. Writing the five is a morning's work and it also has an immediate side benefit: an operation that cannot be described as human steps is usually one that is not actually understood.

The rule to addWhen a new floor or ceiling is added, run it against the existing floor set for the same surface. Any pair that cannot both hold at once gets one row naming which yields, under what condition, and where the tradeoff was decided. A surface that is simultaneously non-compliant in two directions is not a design problem to be re-litigated per session, it is an unarbitrated rule collision, and the fix is one row of text, not another gate.
WhyThe estate's FLOORS LAW rule 5 already demands that every new ceiling name its floor. The symmetric obligation across domains is missing, and the collisions are already live. The imagery floor requires roughly a third of the first viewport to be photographic while the performance law sets LCP at 2.5 seconds and bans an above-fold placeholder strategy, and the two were never reconciled (hierarchy-density-09 names this and stops at the instance). The density floor demands at least four content units plus a cropped fifth on the first mobile viewport, while the type budget caps distinct sizes at four and the emphasis budget caps bold text at 30 percent, which together make a dense card grid arithmetically hard on a 390px screen. Each rule is defensible alone. Nobody owns the pair, so every session resolves it by feel, which is precisely the drift the gates were built to stop.
ProofProject CLAUDE.md FLOORS LAW items 2, 3, 5 and 7, and NEVER-AGAIN item 2. Digest finding hierarchy-density-09 states the imagery/density-versus-LCP conflict was never reconciled; performance-02 confirms the LCP budget exists on paper and is unenforced. Orchestrator section 9 measures the live home page failing four of five floors at once with no record of which one a session should have satisfied first.
Lives inA collisions table at the end of the FLOORS LAW block in the project CLAUDE.md, with the detail in _design-system/LOCKFILE.md
Enforced byAuthoring-time obligation on whoever adds a floor, plus one line in the design-verifier brief: when a screen fails two floors that the collisions table pairs, report it as an arbitration item, not as two defects.
medium A law records the fact its justification depends on, and that fact changing is its review triggerjudge3-15
The rule to addEvery law whose rationale rests on a condition that can change (current data volume, seed content, a one-person team, pre-launch, 28 salons) states that condition in its own row as a dependency. When the condition changes, the row is reviewed, not automatically kept and not automatically dropped. A law with no stated dependency is asserting it is unconditional, and that assertion is itself reviewable.
WhyThe estate's existing endings machinery covers two cases: a newer decision superseding an older one (the supersession tombstone), and a gate being retired. It has no mechanism at all for a rule that quietly stops making sense because the world underneath it moved, which is the most common way law rots in a product that is about to change state completely. Live examples: the density floor's numbers were specified against seeded content, the imagery floor is currently unmeetable because salon_photos has zero rows, and every severity judgement in the estate is currently conditioned on there being no customers. On launch day dozens of rows change meaning at once and nothing marks which ones. This pairs directly with the LAUNCH.md flip list: the dependency fields are what generate that list rather than someone trying to remember.
ProofProject CLAUDE.md density floor ('spec + mock at IDEAL density from SEED data') and imagery floor, both written against seed content; orchestrator live check finds salon_photos with 0 rows for 28 salons and 20 of 28 covers pointing at Unsplash. ~/.claude/LAW_SYSTEM.md section 3.6 covers supersession only; digest finding gate-retirement-policy covers gate disuse only.
Lives inA depends-on field in the _design-system/LOCKFILE.md row format and the _design-system/TASTE_LOG.md entry template, feeding _plans/LAUNCH.md section B
Enforced byAuthoring-time field, plus a one-time backfill pass over the rows whose dependency is obviously pre-launch or seed-data, since those are the ones that all break on the same day.
medium A support promise is published in the Terms and was never sized against one personjudge3-18
The rule to addPublish only the response time one person can keep on their worst week, state it explicitly next to the support address rather than leaving it unsaid, and measure first-response time as one of the numbers from judge3-05. Decide, before launch, the daily booking volume at which manual dispute and support handling stops working, write that number down, and write what happens when it is reached.
WhyThe Terms publish support@solen.ch as the channel for bookings, disputes, refunds and safety reports, with no response time anywhere in the document. That is not a legal problem, it is a capacity problem wearing a legal costume: the same person writes the code, approves the salons, handles the disputes and answers the mail, and the estate has spent 410,000 words on how the product should look and none on how many messages a day that person can absorb. Unstated is also worse than slow: a customer whose stylist did not show up and who hears nothing for two days will chargeback, and a chargeback in this system does not currently update the booking at all (trust-11). Naming a number that can be kept is both the honest promise and the trigger that tells the owner when to stop taking new salons.
Proofapp/[locale]/terms/components/TermsContent.tsx line 8 and line 427 publish support@solen.ch; lines 388-391 describe the reporting channel with no deadline. grep for a response time or SLA in the terms returns nothing. Digest trust-04 independently found there is no refund reporting window either, so both ends of the support promise are open.
Lives inThe Terms of Service contact and dispute sections, plus a capacity line in _plans/LAUNCH.md section A
Enforced byNone mechanical; this is a written promise plus one measured number. The measurement rides on judge3-05's mechanism rather than needing its own.
medium The estate records what was killed and never what Solen is, so scope is defended only by precedentjudge3-20
The rule to addWrite one page, under 300 words, stating what Solen is and what it is not. What it is: booking and payment for Swiss beauty and wellness appointments, for customers who want a specific slot and salons who want that slot filled. What it is not, named explicitly: a salon CRM, a social network, a payments company, a messaging product, a content platform. A proposal that requires Solen to become one of those is rejected on the page, not on precedent. The page is revised only by the owner and its revisions are dated.
WhyThe estate currently defends scope with a graveyard: gift cards, chat, last-minute, Pakete and dog grooming were each individually killed and recorded in REMOVED.md, and the exists-check protocol makes sure a killed thing is not re-proposed. That is a good mechanism for the second time an idea appears and useless for the first, which is when the decision actually costs something. It also puts the owner in the position of being the only filter, one idea at a time, forever. A positive scope statement is the cheapest instrument in this whole report: it lets a session reject a plausible feature on principle, it gives the design law something to serve other than its own consistency, and it is the missing premise behind half the estate's stranded workstreams (a dashboard CRM, a discovery feed, a loyalty system) which are each defensible alone and only questionable against a boundary that was never drawn.
Proof_design-system/REMOVED.md and memory entry project_killed_features.md record gift cards, Pakete UI, last-minute, chat and dog-grooming as individually killed. The project CLAUDE.md exists-check protocol has three layers, all of them backward-looking (what exists, what was removed, hook enforcement). No forward-looking scope statement exists in _docs/, _design-system/ or _plans/.
Lives inA new _docs/WHAT_SOLEN_IS.md, referenced from the top of the project CLAUDE.md and from the exists-check protocol as the check that runs before the graveyard check
Enforced byThe exists-check protocol gains one step ahead of its existing two: does this proposal fit the scope page. No new hook; the ordering is the enforcement, and the page is short enough to be read every time, unlike the 410,000 words behind it.

critical Retired-token enforcement list has drifted from the tokens it is supposed to block color-tokens-01
The rule to addWhenever a token is added to LOCKFILE.md's RETIRED list, the same commit must add the EXACT token name (as it appears in tailwind.config.js) to check.py's RETIRED_TOKENS set, and a CI/pre-commit check must diff the two lists and fail if they disagree. A retired-token name that does not match a real tailwind.config.js key is worse than no entry: it gives false confidence that enforcement exists.
WhyThe drift-checker's RETIRED_TOKENS set is the only mechanical thing standing between 'we said this token is dead' and a new PR quietly reusing it. If the set names tokens that do not exist, it enforces nothing while looking like it enforces something, and nobody notices because the report never fires.

medium The same #6B6B6B grey is reachable through four different token names with no naming-grammar rule to prevent it color-tokens-04
The rule to addA design token's variant (secondary/tertiary/hover/deep) is expressed exactly ONE way per token family: either as a nested Tailwind object key (`s-ink.secondary`) or as a flat hyphen-suffixed sibling token (`s-ink-2`), never both for the same value. When a variant is renamed or collapsed onto another value, the old spelling is deleted from tailwind.config.js in the same change, not left as a second live name for the identical hex.
WhyA token system's entire job is to make 'what color is this and why' answerable by one grep. When one value has multiple legitimate spellings, a future recolor of that grey requires finding and editing every spelling correctly, code review cannot tell whether two different class names are intentionally different shades or accidentally the same, and drift-checking rules (which match by name) silently under- or over-count real usage.
Prooftailwind.config.js line 131 defines `s-ink: { DEFAULT: "#0A0A0A", secondary: "#6B6B6B", tertiary: "#6B6B6B", disabled: "#C5C8C4" }`, and lines 132-133 separately define `s-ink-2: "#6B6B6B"` and `s-ink-3: "#6B6B6B"` -- the exact same hex, four names (`text-s-ink-secondary`, `text-s-ink-tertiary`, `text-s-ink-2`, `text-s-ink-3`). Live usage counts: s-ink-2 appears in 384 files, s-ink-3 in 196 files, s-ink-secondary in 1 file, s-ink-tertiary in 0 files -- so two of the four spellings (s-ink-2 and s-ink-3) are both actively growing in parallel today with zero semantic difference between them, per the tailwind.config.js comment itself ('V3-D138: collapsed onto ink-2').

low No forced-colors / prefers-contrast handling anywhere outside one narrow glass-control note color-tokens-10
The rule to addCore CSS (app/globals.css) declares a `@media (forced-colors: active)` block that lets Windows/Edge High Contrast Mode substitute system colors on backgrounds, borders, and icons that currently rely on Solen's own hex tokens, so that color-dependent affordances (selected-state grey fills, status chips, hairlines) do not visually disappear for a user who has turned on OS-level forced colors.

critical Viewport disables pinch-zoom, defeating WCAG 1.4.4 text resize, and contradicts the estate's own stated WCAG 1.4.4 rationale typography-01
The rule to addThe root viewport export must never set userScalable:false or maximumScale<=1. Pinch-to-zoom stays enabled on every route so a low-vision user can resize text up to 200% per WCAG 1.4.4, even where a fixed-grid layout is the design intent. If specific chrome (a bottom sheet, a sticky nav) must resist accidental double-tap zoom, scope the fix to that element with touch-action, never to the global viewport meta.
WhySetting user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 on the viewport meta tag is the canonical, named WCAG 1.4.4 failure technique (F80 in the WCAG technique catalog): it removes the user's only OS-level way to enlarge text beyond whatever the page's own clamp() ranges allow. Solen's whole type-scale system is built on clamp() and rem-based Tailwind sizing specifically because, per the estate's own RATIONALE.md, that "honors a user's font-size preference (a real WCAG 1.4.4 property)" -- but that preference-honoring machinery is moot if the browser's own zoom gesture is disabled at the root. A user who needs 150% text has no path to it on Solen today.
Proofapp/layout.tsx lines 28-34: `export const viewport: Viewport = { width: "device-width", initialScale: 1, maximumScale: 1, userScalable: false, viewportFit: "cover", themeColor: "#F4F4F6" };` with an adjacent comment explicitly justifying it as locking "the structural UI so accidental pinch-zoom or double-tap doesn't break the grid system." This is the ONE root viewport for the whole site (both /[locale] app routes and dashboard). RATIONALE.md line 142 separately states rem-based scaling exists because it is "a real WCAG 1.4.4 property" honoring user font-size preference -- the two statements sit in the same repo and contradict each other with nobody noticing.
Already therenone. SOURCE.md section 16 (Accessibility rules) has subsections for landmarks, focus, aria, color contrast, touch targets, keyboard nav -- no subsection for text resize or reflow (WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10). RATIONALE.md's WCAG 1.4.4 mention is about the 4px/rem grid, not the viewport meta; it is only a partial, tangential touch on the same success criterion.

The rule to addnext/font weight arrays for every self-hosted family include only the weights the type-law actually permits (400/500/600/700 for Inter Tight, 400/500/600/700 for Inter). Loading a weight the law bans is itself a drift condition: it downloads bytes nobody may legally use and it is the reason the ban keeps getting broken.
WhyA font-weight ban that is unenforced at the loading layer is not a ban, it is a suggestion sitting next to a fully-stocked cabinet. The unused 800/900 weight files for Inter Tight are also pure download weight on every single page load, a CLS/performance cost paid for a typeface cut the design system says is "clumsy" and must never ship.

medium No hyphenation or overflow rule for unbreakable long German compound words inside fixed-width, single-line UI atoms typography-05
The rule to addAny UI atom that must stay single-line by design (a TabPill, a filter chip, a category tag, a button label, a badge) sets `overflow-wrap: break-word` (never `hyphens: auto`, which German needs correctly placed dictionary breaks to avoid mangling a word like Stornierungsbedingungen mid-syllable) OR is explicitly exempted with a documented fallback (truncate + a tooltip / full text on tap) whenever its content is translator-controlled copy, not a fixed short label. A compound-word length check runs against the de.json string for every fixed-width chip/pill/tab component before it ships.
WhySOURCE.md section 17.3 already solves the multi-word-string version of this problem ("always allow text to wrap") but wrapping only works when a string has spaces to break at. A single German compound word has none, so the exact same failure mode SOURCE 17.3 was written to prevent ("assuming text fits in a fixed pixel width") reappears unaddressed the moment the string in question is one long word rather than a short phrase, which is common in German UI copy (policy names, settings labels, legal-document titles).

low Correct font-loading/CLS practice (next/font, display:swap, automatic fallback-metric adjustment) exists in code but is stated nowhere as law typography-07
The rule to addEvery self-hosted font family in the project loads exclusively through next/font (never a manual @font-face or a <link> to a font CDN), keeps Next's automatic fallback-metric adjustment enabled (the default; never pass adjustFontFallback:false), and sets display:'swap' explicitly. This combination is the one and only approved way to add or change a font family, and it is named as a requirement, not left to be inferred from the current file being correct.
WhyThe two mechanisms working together (metric-matched fallback + swap) are what keeps Solen's font swap from causing layout shift: the fallback font is sized to match the real font's metrics, so when Inter Tight/Inter finish downloading, nothing reflows. That is a real, working answer to CLS today, entirely by accident of good original authorship, not by rule -- there is no line anywhere telling a future editor not to regress it (e.g. by adding a third family via a plain <link>, or by disabling the fallback adjustment to 'fix' a rendering quirk). A correct-by-luck state is not durable.
Proofapp/layout.tsx lines 3-14: `import { Inter_Tight, Inter } from "next/font/google"` then `Inter_Tight({ subsets: ["latin"], weight: [...], variable: "--font-inter-tight", display: "swap" })` and the equivalent for Inter -- both correctly configured today. But grep across the whole design-system doc set for the words that would name this as a rule (font-display, size-adjust, CLS, font loading) returns zero hits outside this one file's own inline comments.

LOCKFILE section 2 documents WHICH families and weights to use extensively (V3-D410, the Geist-revert history, the retired-fonts list) but never documents HOW a font must be loaded technically. medium Sticky-positioning plus overflow containing-block interaction has no written law despite a real prior bug layout-geometry-03
The rule to addBefore adding any overflow value other than visible (overflow-hidden, overflow-x-clip, overflow-y-auto, overflow-scroll) to a container, grep its subtree for a `sticky` descendant. Setting overflow to anything but visible on an ancestor creates a new containing block that can silently strip a descendant's ability to pin, independent of that descendant's own sticky/top declaration. Re-verify the sticky element still pins after the change; if it stops pinning, the overflow value on the ancestor is the cause, not the sticky rule itself.
WhyThis is pure CSS mechanics, not taste, which is exactly the kind of rule a reusable law should hold rather than leave to individual memory. It already cost a real fix cycle once (V3-D229), and 55 files in this codebase currently carry a sticky element, meaning the same trap can recur anywhere a future PR adds overflow-hidden to an unrelated section for an unrelated reason.

It was breaking position: sticky on the desktop SalonSidebar , sidebar wrapper had sticky top-24 but couldn't pin because an ancestor with overflow-hidden creates a new containing block that scoped sticky to the wrong context. Result: sidebar scrolled away with the page instead of staying pinned, hiding Termin buchen CTA.' `grep -rln sticky app --include=*.tsx` returns 55 files.

medium No checkable mirror-diff exists for symmetry claims; asymmetric pairs stay a permanent human-eyeball bucket layout-geometry-04
The rule to addA claimed-mirrored pair of elements (a card's left vs right padding, an icon pair flanking a title, twin controls) must pass a reflect-and-diff check: read getComputedStyle on both sides, reflect one about the candidate vertical axis, and assert the resulting padding/margin/position values match within 1px. A failing pair is either a real bug (fix it) or was never meant to be symmetric (name that explicitly in the component's doc so it stops being flagged as broken).
WhySolen's own research already established the perceptual stakes: crude mirror symmetry is judged near pre-attentively (~50ms exposure, Huang/Pashler/Junge 2004, cited at RATIONALE.md:53), so an accidentally-broken mirror reads as a mistake exactly as fast as a designed one reads as intentional. Naming the mechanic in prose is necessary but not sufficient without a way to catch a violation before ship.
ProofThe shipped checker's broken-axis check (per _geometry-triage.md's own class table) only compares sibling EDGE positions (top/left alignment), never left-vs-right padding/margin symmetry around a claimed mirror axis; the triage document's exhaustive class breakdown of all 159 broken-axis findings never surfaces a padding-symmetry comparison, confirming the gap exists in the shipped tool, not only in the docs.

low No law for text vertical-centering by cap-height instead of a font's full line box layout-geometry-07
The rule to addAny button, pill, or badge that vertically centers a single line of text via flex items-center must be checked against the typeface's cap-height-to-baseline box, not its default line box, which carries ascent/descent padding that differs per font and typically reads 1-3px low at UI sizes. Measure the gap from container-top to the glyph's cap-top and from the glyph's baseline to container-bottom in devtools, tune a per-typeface line-height/padding pair once at the highest-traffic size, and reuse that tuned pair everywhere rather than trusting items-center to be correct by default.
WhyThis is a distinct failure mode from the already-locked glyph-overshoot rule: overshoot corrects a glyph sitting off-center inside its OWN box, while this corrects the CONTAINER centering the wrong box (the font's line box, not its visible ink). Both are real, currently unchecked failure modes, but only one of them has a name anywhere in the system.
ProofThe system's two highest-traffic commit buttons (PayConfirmStep.tsx and BookingPaymentForm.tsx, both 52px ink pills) use plain flex items-center with no per-typeface tuning value defined anywhere to check text position against.
Already therenone, and explicitly distinct from the glyph-overshoot rule which IS covered (RATIONALE.md:144, TASTE_LOG.md:187). research/GEOMETRY_PRINCIPLES_2026-07-17.md ADD item 2 named this exact gap by name on 2026-07-17 ('a grep for leading-trim/text-box-trim/cap-height/ascent/descent returns zero hits; this is not a restatement of R5') and it remains unresolved at the time of this audit.

low No scrollbar-gutter law; a scroll container that toggles a scrollbar can shift adjacent content layout-geometry-08
The rule to addAny scroll container whose content height is variable and can cross the scrolling threshold (a modal body, a bottom sheet, a sidebar list) must set scrollbar-gutter: stable, or otherwise reserve the scrollbar's width, so the browser scrollbar's appearance or disappearance never shifts the visible content sideways. Do not rely on overflow-y-auto alone on any container whose content length depends on live data the user can grow (reviews, staff lists, service lists).
WhyThis is a well-documented, classic CSS layout-shift bug (a scrollbar appearing pushes content by roughly 15-17px in a non-overlay-scrollbar environment). It is invisible on macOS' overlay scrollbars, which is plausibly how most design review here happens, but real on Windows and Linux Chrome and inside many embedded webviews, making it exactly the kind of gap that survives visual QA done on one platform and only surfaces once real usage is broader.
ProofAt least 5 distinct modal/sheet/dropdown wrappers in the codebase use max-h-[90vh]/85vh/80vh/60vh combined with overflow-y-auto with no scrollbar-gutter anywhere in app/globals.css; the only scrollbar rule present is scrollbar-width: none (used to fully hide the scrollbar on 2 horizontal carousel rows), which is the opposite tool solving a different problem.
Already therenone.

high The floors gate checks for a comment string, not a measured truth, and was never updated for the EMPHASIS BUDGET numbers hierarchy-density-01
The rule to addAny Stop/PreToolUse gate that claims to enforce a FLOORS LAW item must either (a) programmatically measure the rendered page against the literal in question, or (b) be documented in-repo as a ritual-only check that a downstream verifier-agent pass is mandatory before ship. A gate whose regex only checks for the presence of N characters after the word 'floors:' is not evidence the five-question pass holds, and it currently provides zero coverage of the EMPHASIS BUDGET table (weight-share <=30%, anchor ratio >=1.8x, imagery >=33%, elevation steps >=2) added four days after the gate was written. Every new floor added to LOCKFILE must, in the same commit, either extend an existing gate's checked literal or be named explicitly as verifier-only.
WhyA gate that can be satisfied by writing 'floors: yes all good, checked checked checked checked' creates false confidence that ceilings-without-floors problem (the exact failure UNFINISHED_AUDIT diagnosed) has been fixed at the enforcement layer, when in fact it has only been fixed at the documentation layer. This reproduces the root mechanism the audit itself named: a rule that exists on paper but isn't mechanically checked gets silently skipped under task focus, which is precisely how the 2026-07-25 flatness regression (86% weight-600, 4.7% imagery on home) shipped AFTER the FLOORS LAW was already 'owner-approved' and 'wired'.

The full check at line ~73 is `if FLOORS.search(text): sys.exit(0)` -- pass, no other condition. No reference anywhere in the file to weight share, anchor ratio, imagery percentage, or elevation-step count; the docstring itself only cites LOCKFILE section 17.5 (the original five-question pass, 2026-07-21) and was not touched when the EMPHASIS BUDGET table was added to LOCKFILE on 2026-07-25 (confirmed no second commit to this hook file after that date via its content, which still only mentions the five-question pass).

high No ceiling or display strategy exists for when list data is genuinely RICH (a salon with 80 services, 300 reviews, a 40-photo gallery) hierarchy-density-03

high No trust floor: the finished-screen pass does not require cancellation terms, provider identity, or a price breakdown before a commit action hierarchy-density-05
The rule to addEvery screen carrying a paid commit action (a Bezahlen/pay button, a booking confirmation) must pass a trust floor in addition to the five-question finished-screen pass: (1) the total price is broken down (base + surcharge + VAT if applicable), (2) the cancellation/refund term is visible in the DOM, not merely defined in a labels object, before the commit button, and (3) who the user is booking with (stylist/salon name, not just a category) is visible above the commit action. All three are Pass/Fail gates alongside the existing five.
WhyA booking or payment screen that hits every hierarchy/density floor (a photo, a big number, a semantic color, no dead-grey) can still leave the customer committing money without knowing they can get it back, which is a business-risk gap the FLOORS LAW's aesthetic framing does not touch. WCAG and design-maturity concerns aside, this is a first-principles commerce requirement: Swiss consumer-protection norms and basic marketplace trust both require the cancellation term be visible at the point of commitment, not merely present somewhere in the copy dictionary. Pre-launch framing: this is a gap that would erode trust and likely drive support tickets once real customers pay real money, not a live incident today.

critical Interruptibility is a stated rule with no technical contract, and the default framer-motion pattern used on the highest-traffic surface violates it motion-01
The rule to addAny AnimatePresence wrapping a step-swap, tab-swap, or other frequently-retriggered transition must use mode="popLayout" (or unmounted-immediately exits), never mode="wait". A user acting again mid-transition must see the new content start entering immediately; the outgoing content is allowed to keep exiting underneath it, but it may never gate the incoming content's start. Grep the codebase for AnimatePresence mode="wait" on every PR touching app/**/*.tsx and components*/**/*.tsx; a new instance on a surface a user can retrigger (not a one-shot modal) is a defect, not a style choice.
WhyMOTION.md's THE SPEED LAW hard rule 4 says 'Interruptible. A user acting again mid-motion must not be made to wait for the first one to finish,' and TASTE_MOTION.md finding 18 spends a full section arguing this is the real lever behind 'our product feels static,' bigger than the duration number. But neither document ever says what 'interruptible' means in framer-motion terms. Framer Motion's own AnimatePresence mode="wait" does the literal opposite: it holds the entering child off the DOM until the exiting child's exit animation fully finishes. A rule that says 'must not be made to wait' with no implementation contract is unenforceable, and the codebase proves it: mode="wait" is the dominant pattern, not the exception.
Proofgrep -rn 'AnimatePresence' app --include=*.tsx | grep -i 'mode=' returns 9 hits, all mode="wait": auth/register/page.tsx:299, _components/homepage/SearchBar.tsx:429, _components/homepage/BentoBusiness.tsx:410, _components/search/SearchOverlay.tsx:793 and :865, _components/search/SearchTemplate.tsx:1929, dev/map-motion/page.tsx:205, onboarding/salon/page.tsx:666, dev/search-morph/page.tsx:372. Confirmed live in production code by reading components-legacy/booking/BookingWizard.tsx:213-225 directly: the step content (services -> staff -> datetime -> hair -> pay-confirm, the single flow that converts revenue) is wrapped in `<AnimatePresence mode="wait" custom={1}>` around `variants={stepSwapVariants}` from the shared `useStepSwapMotion()` primitive (motion.ts:166). This is the exact surface TASTE_MOTION finding 18 and LOCKFILE SS16.5 were written to protect, and it is the one place a user is most likely to tap Next twice.
Already therepartial: MOTION.md THE SPEED LAW hard rule 4 and TASTE_MOTION.md finding 18 both assert interruptibility as a principle in prose, but neither names the AnimatePresence mode prop, so there is no way for a reviewer or a gate to check compliance, and the shared primitive that most needs it (useStepSwapMotion) does not comply.

high THE CURVE RULE's own audit missed the shared step-swap primitive: it exits on the entrance curve, not the exit curve motion-02
The rule to addEvery AnimatePresence exit transition must use the accelerate curve (`thud`, cubic-bezier(0.7,0,0.84,0)), never the decelerate curve (`glide`) it entered on. When an enter/exit pair is built as a single shared transition object (one `Transition` reused for both `animate` and `exit`), that reuse is itself the defect: split enter and exit into two transitions with two different eases, even when the other numbers (duration, scale delta) stay identical.
WhyMOTION.md's own THE CURVE RULE (added 2026-07-25, D4 in MOTION_LAW.md) states the assignment explicitly: entering = `glide` decelerate, exiting = `thud` accelerate, and it names four call sites it repointed (Sheet, Modal, Sheet-backdrop on `snap`; Toast on `glide`). It missed a fifth, and it is the highest-traffic one: `useStepSwapMotion` in app/[locale]/_components/primitives/motion.ts is the shared step-swap primitive, and BookingWizard.tsx (the booking flow every paying customer goes through) is its real call site. A rule that ships with a fix list and misses its own most-used primitive means the audit method (grep for named tokens) did not catch a primitive that reuses one Transition object for both directions.
Proofapp/[locale]/_components/primitives/motion.ts:166-181 (useStepSwapMotion): `const stepSwapTransition: Transition = { duration: STEP_SWAP_DURATION, ease: GLIDE_EASE };` is declared once (line 138) and reused for both `animate` (center) and `exit` (return statement, line 178-179: `transition: stepSwapTransition` applied uniformly across the whole Variants object). components-legacy/booking/BookingWizard.tsx:213-225 confirms the real call site: `const { variants: stepSwapVariants, transition: stepSwapTransition } = useStepSwapMotion();` then `<AnimatePresence mode="wait" custom={1}><motion.div variants={stepSwapVariants} initial="enter" animate="center" exit="exit" transition={stepSwapTransition}>`. Every booking step that slides out is decelerating on the way out, the exact 'visibly slows down leaving' defect MOTION.md itself uses to describe the Toast bug it already fixed.

high The stagger recipe has no ceiling: past 8 items, new cards enter at the same instant as the first card, on the app's own largest feed motion-03
The rule to addEvery stagger container must define a hard ceiling (a maximum stagger-eligible index, e.g. 8) AND an explicit overflow rule for items beyond it: either (a) cap all items beyond the ceiling at the LAST defined delay (so item 9+ enters together with item 8, never with item 1), or (b) disable per-item stagger entirely past the ceiling and let the remainder enter as one group at the ceiling's delay. A stagger utility that silently falls back to a delay of 0 for unenumerated children is a defect, because 0 means 'enters with the very first item,' the opposite of graceful degradation.
WhyA cascading entrance is legible because each item's delay is monotonically later than the one before it. When the CSS only enumerates delays for a fixed number of children and every unenumerated child inherits the undeclared default (0ms, same as the FIRST child), items beyond the ceiling do not degrade to 'no stagger', they degrade to 'wrong stagger': they appear to jump the queue and enter alongside item 1, ahead of items 2 through 8. On a results grid this reads as visual noise or a rendering glitch, the exact 'raggedy' quality the ENTER RECIPE was built to eliminate for single-element entrances.
Proofapp/globals.css:526-538: `.salon-card-stagger > *` sets the shared keyframe animation with no delay, then `:nth-child(1)` through `:nth-child(8)` override animation-delay from 0ms to 350ms in 50ms steps; there is no rule for :nth-child(9) or beyond, so those children keep the base rule's implicit animation-delay: 0ms (browser default), identical to :nth-child(1). app/[locale]/_components/search/SearchTemplate.tsx:140 sets `const PAGE_SIZE = 12;` and line 1616 applies the `salon-card-stagger` class to the results grid that renders up to PAGE_SIZE items per page. So on the single feed in the app most likely to render more than 8 items at once (search results), cards 9 through 12 enter at t=0, simultaneously with card 1, ahead of cards 2-8.

medium No contract for animating a list that reorders under the user without an error or a full refetch motion-08
The rule to addWhen an already-rendered list's item ORDER changes while the surface is visible and no error/refetch cycle is involved (a live queue position update, a re-sort after a background price/availability change, a realtime rank change), the transition must preserve each item's visual continuity: measure its old position, let it animate (transform-only) to its new position over the snap tier (150ms), and never unmount/remount the row or silently teleport it. This is a distinct case from Pattern 5 (stale/refreshing, where the whole surface's DATA is stale) and from the realtime-mismatch error branch (a toast plus a 3-second auto-refresh); reordering the same, still-valid data is neither an error nor staleness, and treating it as one produces an unnecessary toast or a jarring full redraw for a normal, expected event.
WhySolen already has at least one live, real-time-driven ranked list (the walk-in queue tracker) and multiple sortable browse surfaces where the ranking can legitimately change while a user is looking (a filter narrowing results, a live availability drop). The motion-22 vocabulary table has an entry for a NUMBER changing in place ('Live position/number updates -> departure-board flip .animate-num-flip'), which covers the digit inside one row updating, but nothing covers the DOM position of that row changing relative to its siblings, which is a different animation problem (a FLIP-style transform, not a text-flip). Left unspecified, the two plausible default behaviors, a silent instant reflow or a full list re-render, are both worse than a position-preserving transition: one produces the 'items silently teleport' bug, the other looks like data loss.
Proof_design-system/components/LoadingStates.md Pattern 5 (lines 227-243, read in full): covers only the case where the SAME items stay in place and the surface indicates a background refetch (thin progress bar, old data stays at 100% opacity); its anti-pattern list explicitly forbids replacing rendered data with skeletons, but says nothing about a rank change. LoadingStates.md's error-source table (line 159) has one row for 'Realtime sync mismatch: Toast + auto-refresh after 3s', which is a CONFLICT-resolution path (something is now wrong), not a graceful in-place reorder. MOTION.md's motion-22 table (line 114) has 'Live position/number updates | departure-board flip | .animate-num-flip', confirmed by grep to key on a single number's value, not on a DOM-order swap between rows.

low Motion complexity never degrades for device capability, only for explicit user opt-in motion-09
The rule to addOn top of `prefers-reduced-motion` (a user's explicit request), the app should read at least one coarse, cheap device-capability signal (`navigator.hardwareConcurrency`, `navigator.deviceMemory`, or `navigator.connection.saveData`/`effectiveType`) once per session and, below a named threshold, drop the expensive tier of the motion stack (blur filters on entrance, simultaneous stagger, non-essential spring physics) while KEEPING the cheap tier (opacity/transform press feedback, the snap-tier state flips). This is a distinct control from prefers-reduced-motion: a capable device with an unbothered user should keep the full recipe; a genuinely low-end device should get a lighter recipe even if the user never touched an accessibility setting.
WhyTHE SPEED LAW and THE ENTER RECIPE were captured and tuned against an iPhone UA in a Playwright 390x844 viewport, a mid-to-high-end reference device; the marketplace's own positioning (mid-market, price-sensitive Swiss salons and their customers) does not guarantee that device class on the customer side, and a blur filter plus a scale transform plus opacity, animated across a 12-item stagger, is real compositor and paint work that a low-end Android handles measurably worse than the capture device. Without a capability-based fallback, the ONLY lever a struggling device has is the same one a user with vestibular sensitivity has (prefers-reduced-motion), which conflates two unrelated needs and requires a user to know a system setting exists rather than the app adapting on its own.
Proofgrep -c 'prefers-reduced-motion' app/globals.css -> 11 occurrences, confirming reduced-motion IS wired broadly. grep -rln 'hardwareConcurrency\|navigator.connection\|deviceMemory\|effectiveType' app lib (excluding node_modules) -> zero hits anywhere in the codebase; no capability-based branch exists at all, in any file, for any surface.
Already therenone: prefers-reduced-motion is the only motion-scaling lever documented or built anywhere in the estate; there is no capability-based tier at all.

high Double-submit protection uses a real mutex (ref) in exactly one flow; everywhere else it is React-state-only, which has a known race states-forms-05
The rule to addAny control that triggers a non-idempotent write (create booking, create payment intent, submit a review, send a refund request) must guard against a double-fire with a synchronous ref/lock checked BEFORE the async call starts, not only a React state flag used to disable the button, because state-only disabling can still race a fast double-click/double-tap ahead of the re-render that disables the control. high No EXIF/GPS metadata stripping on any photo upload path imagery-icons-01
The rule to addEvery image uploaded by a user (salon gallery, review photo, service photo, client progress photo, profile avatar) must have EXIF metadata, including GPS coordinates and device identifiers, stripped server-side before the file is written to Storage or served publicly. No uploaded image byte stream reaches a public bucket unprocessed.
WhyA phone photo carries GPS coordinates and device metadata by default. A salon owner uploading a gallery photo from their own phone (at home, before opening the shop) or a customer uploading a review photo can unknowingly publish their home address or device fingerprint to a public bucket that anyone can download and inspect. This is a live privacy leak from day one of public launch, not a hypothetical.
ProofRead app/api/salons/[slug]/gallery/route.ts, app/api/reviews/[id]/photos/route.ts, app/api/services/[id]/photos/route.ts, app/api/clients/[id]/photos/route.ts end to end: every one of the four upload routes does `formData.get("file")` -> MIME/size check -> `supabase.storage.from(<bucket>).upload(path, file)` directly. No `sharp`, no `exif`, no metadata-stripping step anywhere in the call chain. `grep -n '"sharp"' package.json` returns nothing; the package is not even a dependency.

high 35 raw <img> tags on customer surfaces bypass next/image, including the locked global Avatar primitive imagery-icons-04
The rule to addEvery image whose src the app controls (any Supabase Storage URL, any remote allowlisted host) renders through next/image, never a raw <img>, on any customer-facing route. A raw <img> is permitted only for content next/image structurally cannot handle (HTML email templates, or a data: URI generated client-side).
Whynext/image is the only mechanism in this codebase that gives automatic responsive srcset generation, format negotiation, and lazy-loading by default. A raw <img> gets none of that: it ships the full-resolution original at every viewport width, which directly works against the imagery floor (LOCKFILE + CLAUDE.md require photos to be ~1/3 of the customer viewport) by making the heaviest-imagery screens also the least optimized ones.
Proofgrep -rn '<img ' app returns 35 hits, and next/image import count is 33. Customer-facing (not dev/) files using raw <img>: SalonPortfolio.tsx:123, SalonImageGallery.tsx:232, ProfileTabs.tsx (5 instances), queue/[token]/page.tsx (3 instances), RecentlyViewedClient.tsx, walk-in-pay/page.tsx, inspo/page.tsx, inspo/board/[id]/page.tsx, and critically primitives/Avatar.tsx:74 -- the ONE component COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md calls 'the canonical avatar for any person/salon avatar' and lists as used at 5+ production call-sites (reviews, staff carousel, staff profile) -- meaning every staff and reviewer photo across the whole product ships unoptimized.

medium Alt text has no authoring rule and is empty on informative content images imagery-icons-03
The rule to addEvery image tag decides, at write time, whether it is decorative (alt="" is correct) or informative (alt must describe the depicted content, never just repeat the salon name that is already visible as text next to it). A content photo the user can open, save, or scroll through (portfolio grid tile, saved-salon tile, gallery swipe photo) always carries a real alt describing what the photo shows; only chrome/icon-glyph images get alt="".

medium No image weight (KB) budget or compression pipeline for user-uploaded photos imagery-icons-06
The rule to addEvery image accepted from a salon owner or customer is re-encoded server-side to a bounded maximum file size (for example, 300KB at the largest served dimension) before it is written to Storage, independent of the raw upload's original size. The 5MB upload cap is an INPUT ceiling, not a served-weight guarantee.
WhyThe upload routes only cap the ORIGINAL file at 5MB; nothing re-encodes or compresses it afterward. A phone photo at or near that 5MB ceiling, uploaded through a raw <img> tag (finding imagery-icons-04) with no next/image optimization layer, is served to every visitor at its original weight. On a photo-heavy marketplace where the imagery floor requires photos to cover roughly a third of every viewport, this compounds directly into slow LCP and real mobile data cost for Swiss users on limited plans.

high Multi-step booking wizard has no browser-back / gesture-back contract ia-navigation-01
The rule to addAny multi-step flow that is implemented as in-memory state rather than separate routes (the booking wizard) must intercept the browser/gesture back navigation the same way it intercepts the in-app exit control: either push one history entry per step so physical back steps the wizard back logically, or attach a popstate/beforeunload guard that shows the same 'leave this booking?' confirmation the X button already shows. A step transition that is invisible to the browser's own history stack is not a complete step.
WhyThe wizard already treats losing progress as serious enough to earn a dedicated confirm-guard component for one exit path (the X button). If the physical back button or an edge-swipe (both standard mobile gestures) silently discard the same in-progress selections with zero warning, the product is inconsistent about how much it protects the same user state, and the inconsistency is invisible until a real user swipes back mid-flow and loses everything with no way to know it happened.
Proofcomponents-legacy/booking/BookingWizard.tsx:115 reads currentStep/goToStep from useBooking() (React context state only); lib/booking-context.tsx has zero occurrences of popstate, sessionStorage, or localStorage (grepped, no hits); components-legacy/booking/BookingExitButton.tsx implements a 'leave this booking?' confirm guard (its own doc-comment cites Fresha IMG_4831) but that guard fires only on the explicit X click, never on router-level navigation; _docs/FRONTEND.md:293 documents that ONLY step-1's in-app back arrow does router.back(), steps 2+ use an in-app goToStep() with no browser-history entry at all.

medium Auth-interrupt login redirect does not universally preserve the user's destination ia-navigation-03
The rule to addEvery place that redirects an unauthenticated user to /auth/login because they attempted a gated action (not a generic 'login' nav click) MUST append `?redirect=<the page or the specific action's return path>`, using the encodeURIComponent'd current pathname, exactly as the majority of /profile/* server pages already do. A login redirect with no `redirect=` param is only acceptable when the user explicitly navigated to a generic auth entry point (a 'Log in' menu link), never when their own in-context action (save, book, look up) is what triggered the redirect.
WhyThis project already got most of this right: 18 of 19 /profile/* pages use a server-side redirect() with an encoded `redirect=` param, and the login page (components-legacy/auth/SignIn.tsx:30-49) correctly reads it back and validates it's an internal relative path before honoring it (open-redirect protection is already solved). The remaining three call sites are exactly the highest-friction ones: a user hearting a look, looking up a booking by code, or opening an intake form gets bounced to a blank login screen and, after authenticating, lands on the homepage instead of back where they were, forcing them to re-find and redo the action that prompted login in the first place.

medium No scroll-restoration law or implementation exists anywhere in the app ia-navigation-05
The rule to addAny list/grid page a user can navigate away from and back to (search results, Inspo feed, saved items) must restore the user's exact scroll position on back-navigation, not reset to top. This is implemented via a scroll-position cache keyed by pathname+querystring (sessionStorage or Next's own scroll-restoration primitive), restored in a layout-level effect, not left to the browser's default (which App Router's client-side transitions do not reliably preserve).
WhyLosing scroll position on back-navigation from a detail page to a list is one of the most common, most-noticed navigation papercuts in any browse-then-inspect product (this is literally the 'return-to-spot' task class Nielsen Norman group names for infinite scroll specifically). The rule to addWhen a route is killed, its outcome must be chosen from ONE named decision tree, not improvised per feature: (a) the concept moved and still exists under a new URL -> `permanentRedirect()` (308) to the new location; (b) the concept is gone but a nearby page is still the right landing spot -> a plain `redirect()` to that page; (c) the concept is entirely gone with no landing spot -> the route is deleted and MUST be added to `COMING_SOON_ROUTES`-style middleware list or otherwise produce the locked 404 page, never a bare unstyled Next.js default 404. Every REMOVED.md entry for a route deletion must state which of the three it chose and why.
WhyA user or bookmark hitting a killed route should get a predictable class of outcome (redirected forward, redirected to safety, or a designed 404), never a coin-flip depending on which engineer happened to delete that particular feature. Right now the SAME repo has all three outcomes live for three different killed features with no record of why each got a different treatment, which means the choice was never actually a choice, it was whatever felt convenient that day.

The rule to addA URL query parameter name carries exactly ONE meaning across the entire app. Once `category` means 'service taxonomy' on /search, no other route may use `category` to mean something else (a discovery vertical); if a second, genuinely distinct concept needs a similarly-named param, it gets a feature-scoped or explicitly disambiguated name (`discoveryCategory`, or a documented shared enum) instead of reusing the bare word.

Having the URL layer use the same bare param name (`category`) for both taxonomies on two different routes is the exact kind of surface-level collision that makes the underlying, already-known semantic split easy to get wrong: copy a `category=nails` query string from an Inspo link into a /search-shaped context (or vice versa, e.g. a future shared search-and-discover surface) and it silently resolves against the wrong taxonomy instead of erroring.

Responsive and desktop
