high The FLOORS LAW (imagery third, emphasis budget, display anchor) has no desktop measurement, by explicit hardcoded design responsive-desktop-01
The rule to addEvery floor in CLAUDE.md's NEVER-AGAIN and FLOORS LAW blocks (imagery >= 33% of first viewport, display anchor >= 28px, weight-share <= 30%, anchor ratio >= 1.8x) must be re-measured and re-thresholded for the desktop viewport (1280x900) and the tablet viewport (768x1024), not only for 390x844. A floor computed as a percentage of viewport area or a fixed px anchor does not transfer: the same photo at the same px size is a much smaller share of a 1280-wide viewport than a 390-wide one, and a 28px display anchor that looks dominant on a 390px screen can read as an afterthought on a 1280px one. Each floor needs either a per-viewport threshold table or an explicit, named statement that the floor is mobile-only and desktop is out of scope for that specific check.
WhyA floor that is only checked at one width is not a floor, it is a mobile-only spot-check wearing a floor's name. The system already tracks 45/422 (10.6%) of tsx files with an lg:/xl: variant, meaning most desktop rendering is either literally the same DOM stretched wider (in which case the mobile-measured floor happens to still roughly hold) or genuinely different (in which case nothing verifies it). Given the density floor in CLAUDE.md already gives a DIFFERENT number for desktop (>= 6 units vs >= 4 mobile) for exactly this reason, the same viewport-sensitivity logic was already recognized for ONE floor and never generalized to the others.
Proofscripts/check-geometry.mjs:101-103 defines VIEWPORTS = {mobile: 375x812, tablet: 768x1024, desktop: 1280x900} and accepts --viewport, but its own comment block at lines 142-151 states: 'Measures the FLOORS LAW / EMPHASIS BUDGET literals, on the RENDERED first viewport at 390x844 (fixed, independent of --viewport...)' and the constant is literally named FLOORS_VIEWPORT = { width: 390, height: 844 } (line 152), separate from and never fed by the VIEWPORTS map used for checks (a)-(d). npm run check:floors / gate:floors (package.json lines 15-16) both call --floors-only, which always uses this fixed 390x844 viewport regardless of any --viewport flag passed.
Already therepartial: the density floor (CLAUDE.md FLOORS LAW 3, design contract 'density floor' row) is the ONE floor that already carries a desktop-specific number (6 vs 4). The delta is that imagery (F2), display anchor (F6), weight-share (F7a) and anchor-ratio (F7b), all defined in the same FLOORS LAW block and all measured by the same check-geometry.mjs script, do not.

It does not cover the functional case, where losing the hover reveal makes an action literally impossible to trigger on a touch device, a dead click by omission rather than commission. The gap is proven live in the calendar editor, a surface operators plausibly run on an iPad at a salon front desk.

critical No visible focus indicator survives on any non-input control, and no substitute was ever mandated accessibility-01
The rule to addEvery focusable interactive element that is not a text input (link, button, pill, tab, icon-button, summary, [role=button], [tabindex]) must render a visible, non-color-only state change on :focus-visible with at least 3:1 contrast against its adjacent colors (WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured Minimum, and the base 2.4.7 Focus Visible, both AA). If a ring/outline stays banned for aesthetic reasons, ONE approved non-ring alternative (ink background fill, underline extension, or the border-color shift THE INPUT FOCUS LAW already uses for inputs) must be defined and wired globally for chrome elements the same way inputs already got one. A resting state of zero visible change on keyboard focus is never acceptable, ring or no ring.
WhyA sighted keyboard user (motor-impaired, or anyone tabbing instead of pointing) currently gets no signal of which link, button, pill, or tab is about to activate on the next Enter/Space press anywhere except a text input. That is not a smaller version of accessibility, it is its total absence on every button and link in the product.
Proofapp/globals.css:387-393 sets `outline:none` unconditionally on `a:focus, a:focus-visible, button:focus, button:focus-visible, [role="button"]:focus-visible, [tabindex]:focus-visible, summary:focus-visible` for ALL devices (not touch-only; the touch-only carve-out is a separate, later block at :407-420). The code's own comment at :381-382 states plainly 'this drops the WCAG 2.4.7 keyboard focus indicator on chrome, owner call.' Only `input:focus-visible, textarea:focus-visible, select:focus-visible` (globals.css:1255-1264+) keep any focus treatment. The ONE a11y-adjacent enforcement hook in the whole estate, `~/.claude/hooks/no-focus-ring-gate.py`, exists to BLOCK re-adding a ring; there is no counterpart gate that requires any substitute indicator, so the estate's only automated a11y control currently enforces the ring's absence, not the requirement it replaces.

RATIONALE.md:119 is the only place that honestly records the current state as 'a recorded owner tradeoff, not an oversight' for links/buttons specifically. The delta the existing text does not say: no doc anywhere prescribes what the REQUIRED substitute treatment is, and none of SOURCE/CLAUDE.md/LOCKFILE have been reconciled with the current CSS, so a future contributor reading section 16.2 or the CLAUDE.md contract row would ship believing a focus ring still exists.

high Viewport meta disables pinch-zoom sitewide accessibility-03
The rule to addNever set `maximumScale` below a value that blocks zoom, and never set `userScalable: false`, on any page's viewport meta. Structural-UI protection against accidental pinch-zoom belongs on the specific gesture-sensitive element (`touch-action` CSS on a map or gallery), never on the document-level viewport, because disabling the OS pinch gesture for the whole page is WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text (AA) technique failure F102, and it removes the ONLY zoom mechanism low-vision users on Android Chrome have (iOS Safari has ignored the flag since iOS 10, so this bites Android specifically, silently).
WhyA low-vision user on the largest global mobile OS by device count needs pinch-zoom to read anything the site's own text-size scale does not already cover; disabling it removes their only fallback, and the comment justifying it (preventing 'accidental pinch-zoom' on the structural grid) is solved elsewhere in the same file with `touch-action` on individual elements, so the sitewide block buys nothing the local fix didn't already cover.
Proofapp/layout.tsx:29-32: `export const viewport: Viewport = { width: "device-width", initialScale: 1, maximumScale: 1, userScalable: false, viewportFit: "cover" }`. The adjacent comment (lines 24-28) explicitly frames this as intentional: 'maximumScale=1 + userScalable=false locks the structural UI... Content pinch-zoom on specific elements (photos, maps) still works via touch-action: pinch-zoom on those elements if needed' - i.e. the codebase already has the correct narrow-scope tool and used the wrong, page-wide one anyway.

high No contrast-ratio gate exists, and the system has already authorized a sub-threshold grey for informational text accessibility-05
The rule to addNo text color token may be authorized for use on prose, labels, timestamps, hints, or placeholders below a computed 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its target background (3:1 only for text at or above 18pt/24px or 14pt/18.5px bold, per WCAG 1.4.3 AA). The contrast ratio must be computed and recorded in the SAME commit that authorizes a token for text use, not asserted from vibes. A token that fails 4.5:1 is restricted by definition to genuinely non-text use (dividers, disabled-icon fills) that 1.4.3 exempts, and that restriction must be written into the token's own row, not left to a component author's judgment call at build time.
Why'Non-load-bearing' is not a WCAG exemption category: a timestamp, a placeholder, or a hint is still text a sighted low-vision user needs to read, and 1.4.3 does not distinguish 'important' text from 'hint' text, only text from decoration. Authorizing a color this far under threshold for exactly the text types (timestamps, hints, placeholders) users most often squint at is backwards.
ProofComputed directly: contrast(#9CA3AF, #FFFFFF) = 2.54:1, contrast(#9CA3AF, #F4F4F5) = 2.31:1, both far under the 4.5:1 AA floor and even under the 3:1 large-text floor. CLAUDE.md's FLOORS LAW block (the pinned block in this very repo's root CLAUDE.md, display-anchor row) states: 'Tertiary grey #9CA3AF (s-chart-2) is reinstated for NON-load-bearing text only (chevrons, placeholders, timestamps, hints)... forbidden on load-bearing copy' - i.e. the estate's own live governing doc explicitly authorizes 2.54:1 grey for exactly the text categories 1.4.3 does not exempt. Current usage is 0 (`grep -rn 'text-s-chart-2' app components` -> 0 hits), so this has not shipped live yet, but the law is armed and would ship an inaccessible token the next time someone builds a timestamp or hint using it, believing it's sanctioned.
Already therepartial: SOURCE.md section 16.4 documents contrast ratios for the ORIGINAL token set as a one-time table, correctly computed for those pairs, but it is not a gate, has never been re-run against tokens added later (s-ink-2/#6B6B6B is fine at 5.33:1, s-chart-2/#9CA3AF is not and was never checked against it), and LOCKFILE.md's own s-chart-2 definition scopes it to 'bar/line/area charts' ONLY, which the CLAUDE.md FLOORS LAW block then contradicts by re-authorizing it for prose. The delta: no mechanism catches a future token or a future rule that reopens a failing color for text.

critical refundFlow namespace (261/264 keys) is English-only in de/fr/it, with a live _todo_translate marker ignored for 7+ weeks copy-i18n-01
The rule to addAny namespace containing a boolean or non-string sentinel key (e.g. `_todo_translate: true`) fails CI immediately: a pre-merge script scans every messages/*.json for non-string leaf values and non-en locale files whose string value is byte-identical to the en.json value at the same key, and blocks merge until the count is zero or the key is added to a named, dated allowlist. A namespace may not ship customer-facing (i.e. reachable outside /dev) until every locale's translator-facing string differs from the English placeholder or is explicitly allowlisted with an owner-approved reason.
WhyA TODO marker that lives only as data (a JSON key) with no code path that reads it and fails is invisible to every existing gate (typecheck, lint, invariants) and to the human eye unless someone opens the raw JSON. Additionally, any single-line, fixed-height control (the locked `h-11` button/pill/icon-button row in the design contract) must be verified, per translated string, to not wrap or clip: either the button grows to two lines gracefully by design, or the string is measured against the button's max width in all four locales before the key ships.

high Total-price law has no Swiss PBV legal floor, only a UX-conversion framing ethics-psychology-01
The rule to addEvery price shown to a Swiss consumer at the moment a booking becomes a purchase offer (the first screen where a service price appears, not just at Bezahlen) must be the actual total price payable in CHF, including VAT and any non-optional surcharge, per Preisbekanntgabeverordnung (PBV) Art. 10 and SECO's own clarification that hidden, link-only, or checkout-only price components do not satisfy disclosure. This is a legal floor, independent of and stricter in enforcement risk than the conversion-motivated 'relative label only if small and next to the absolute price' allowance in PSYCHOLOGY.md law 5, and the file must say so explicitly rather than reading as a pure A/B-testable optimization.
WhyPSYCHOLOGY.md law 5 was derived entirely from Baymard abandonment research, a UX metric, not from Swiss law. If a future add-on or surcharge feature leans on the 'relative label ... only when genuinely small' allowance without independently satisfying PBV's own total-price-at-the-purchase-offer-moment test, Solen risks a SECO or Lauterkeitskommission enforcement action regardless of any conversion outcome. A legal floor and a UX best practice can diverge, and only one carries a fine or injunction risk; right now they are written as if they are the same rule.
ProofPSYCHOLOGY.md line 28 (law 5): 'Add-on prices may use a relative label ("2.9% des Preises") ONLY directly next to the visible absolute price, only when genuinely small and fair.' No PBV, SECO, or Preisbekanntgabeverordnung citation anywhere in the file. bookings.platform_fee (lib/types.ts:244, app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts:155) is currently a salon-side commission taken via Stripe application_fee, not a customer-facing line item, but the code path and the relative-label allowance both exist, and nothing stops a future customer-facing surcharge from leaning on the allowance without a PBV check.

The gap is that the file never names PBV as a separate, non-negotiable legal floor, so the relative-label carve-out reads as tunable UX policy rather than something bounded by law.

The rule to addEvery user-facing consent or preference toggle (notification category switches, marketing opt-in, a future personalization opt-out) must have at least one automated check proving a real send-path reads that exact column before the toggle ships, using the same discriminate-the-behavior standard CLAUDE.md already requires for search filters ('a filter must DISCRIMINATE... not just render or return 200'). A consent flag that renders and saves but is never read by the code that actually sends is not a UX-bug-tier issue; it is a false consent claim to the user, and should be treated with the same severity as a security silent no-op, not a cosmetic defect.
WhyCLAUDE.md's existing silent-no-op doctrine is written entirely around search and filter correctness (PostgREST swallowing a bad column, isOpenNow reading the wrong day-keys); it never names CONSENT flags as a distinct case, even though a consent flag that silently does nothing is a materially worse failure than a silent filter: the user is told 'you turned this off' while an entirely separate code path with no such check keeps contacting them. The rule to addAny automated mass marketing communication (SMS, push, email) to a Swiss consumer requires the recipient's prior, verifiable opt-in before the first send, per UWG Art. 3 Abs. 1 lit. o; sending on an opt-out-by-default basis is an unfair-competition offense carrying up to three years imprisonment or a fine under UWG Art. 23, not merely a retention-metric risk. Solen's marketing-category defaults must be documented as satisfying this opt-in requirement by design (default OFF, per PSYCHOLOGY.md law 14), and any future proposal to flip a marketing category on-by-default must be flagged as a legal question first, never shipped as a normal growth A/B test.

That framing invites a purely growth-metrics argument for turning a category on by default if the measured opt-out rate looks tolerable, when in Switzerland doing so for non-transactional marketing sends without prior consent is a criminal unfair-competition offense regardless of the resulting opt-out percentage. The current default-off setting happens to comply, but the file gives no reason a future engineer or growth push could not treat it as a soft UX preference and override it.

WebSearch confirmed UWG Art. 3(1)(o) requires prior, documented opt-in for automated mass marketing via telecom channels, with criminal exposure under Art. 23 UWG.

critical Salon phone verification is a silent no-op: promised in the ToS, faked by the code trust-01-phone-verification-silent-noop
The rule to addAny account attribute the Terms of Service represent to users as verified (phone, email, business identity) must be written to the database by the same request that confirms it, and no admin approval action may activate an account while that field is still false. A verification endpoint that returns `verified:true` without persisting a corresponding DB write is a defect, not a deferred feature, and ships blocked until fixed.
WhyUsers and salon partners read `verified` badges and ToS promises as a factual claim about safety. If the code that is supposed to make the claim true instead simulates success and quietly skips the write, the platform is asserting something false to every customer who trusts a verified salon, and the founder has no record of what was actually checked if a dispute or fraud case ever needs it.
Proofapp/api/auth/verify-phone/check/route.ts:56-63: the OTP check succeeds, deletes the Redis code, and returns `{verified:true}` with a comment admitting 'They will do that in the POST /api/salons handler when they submit the form.' app/api/salons/route.ts:696 is that handler, and the write is commented out: `// phone_verified: phone_verified || false, // [FIX] Bypassing schema cache error (defaults to false in DB)`. Also app/api/auth/verify-phone/check/route.ts:35-38: when UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL/TOKEN are unset, the endpoint returns 'Verifiziert (Simuliert - Redis fehlt)' for ANY code, no OTP check at all. Separately, app/api/admin/salons/[id]/approve/route.ts:24-37 (the admin approve action) never reads phone_verified or salon_documents at all before setting `is_active:true`, so even a correctly-written phone_verified would not currently gate activation.

critical Per-salon cancellation/no-show fee has no code ceiling matching the ToS-promised platform cap trust-02-cancellation-fee-ceiling-unenforced

If the ToS number and the validation ceiling ever diverge, the ToS text is the one to change, not the other way around, and the change follows the ToS-amendment notice process in the same document.
WhyA marketplace's written cancellation/no-show terms are the one promise customers rely on before entering a card. If any individual salon can quietly set a stricter policy than what every customer was told applies platform-wide, the platform is exposed to a straightforward Swiss consumer-protection and false-advertising claim the moment real money starts moving, and it erodes exactly the trust the two-sided marketplace depends on.

high No refund/appeal reporting window exists in writing or in code, leaving indefinite reopenable liability trust-04-no-refund-reporting-window
The rule to addA marketplace's refund/complaint policy must state a maximum number of days after service delivery during which a customer may open a money-back case, and the booking_disputes creation endpoint must enforce that window server-side (reject a new case opened outside it, absent a documented exception like a chargeback). Pick the number once, write it in the ToS, and make the code match it exactly.

Backend, security and data

79 missing principles across 8 topics.

Auth, roles, RLS

10
critical Live RLS hole: an orphaned permissive UPDATE policy neutralizes every later restriction on reviews authz-rls-01
The rule to addWhen a new, more restrictive RLS policy is added to replace overly-permissive write access on a table, the migration that adds it must DROP the old permissive policy for the same command in the same migration, and this must be verified by a one-time query (not a memory) confirming exactly one permissive policy remains per (table, command) pair unless the OR-combination is a deliberate, named design. Postgres RLS combines multiple PERMISSIVE policies for the same command with OR, so an old USING(true) policy is never narrowed by a newer, stricter one added later; it must be explicitly retired.
WhyPostgres evaluates all applicable PERMISSIVE policies for a command as an OR: a row passes if ANY one of them allows it. A team that reasons 'we tightened this with a new policy' without checking for surviving old ones ships a control that looks fixed in code review (the diff shows a new, correct policy) while being unfixed in the database (the old catch-all is still live and wins the OR). This is exactly the same 'looks wired, does nothing' failure class this project has already named as its number one problem (silent no-ops), just at the DDL layer instead of the query layer, which is why it is invisible to code review and to every grep that only looks at the newest migration.
Proofsupabase/migrations/005_reviews_trust.sql:29-31 creates `CREATE POLICY IF NOT EXISTS "Owners can update review replies" ON reviews FOR UPDATE USING (true) WITH CHECK (true);` with no TO clause (applies to every role Postgres grants UPDATE to on this table, which by Supabase's default bootstrap GRANTs is both anon and authenticated). supabase/migrations/029_review_policies.sql:4-7 later adds the intended real restriction, `CREATE POLICY "reviews_update_own_48h" ON public.reviews FOR UPDATE USING (auth.uid() = user_id AND created_at > now() - interval '48 hours')`, clearly meant to be the actual rule (own review, 48h window). Because Postgres ORs permissive policies, the 005 policy still applies and its USING/WITH CHECK are both `true`, so the 029 restriction is decorative: any client holding a valid anon or authenticated Supabase key can UPDATE any column (rating, review text, is_flagged, booking_id, owner_reply, etc.) on ANY row of the reviews table for ANY salon, via a direct PostgREST call that never touches this app's route handlers at all. _design-system/REMOVED.md's 2026-07-25 entry ('reviews-reply-route...') confirms the APP-layer write path to owner_reply/salon_response was already retired as dead, which the owner may have believed closed this surface; it did not, because the vulnerable object is the table-wide RLS policy, not the app route, and the policy was never touched by that cleanup.
Already therenone: research/authz.md section 3-4 covers IDOR and tenant isolation as prose principles but was written from a table/policy COUNT (326 CREATE POLICY statements exist) never from a per-table, per-command AUDIT of what those policies actually combine to allow. No gate, lint, or checklist item checks for more than one permissive policy per (table, command).

FOR <cmd>) and fails when a table has more than one PERMISSIVE policy for the same command unless the pair is listed in an explicit allowlist naming why the OR is intentional. Also runnable as a one-time manual audit before it becomes a script.

high The `staff` role is authorization-unmodeled at every layer and is actively locked out of the surface it exists for authz-rls-02
The rule to addEvery value in profiles.role must have a written authorization invariant, enforced identically at the route/middleware layer and the RLS layer, before any UI or invite flow that grants that role ships. A role that can be assigned to a user but has no corresponding RLS predicate and no route-layer allowlist is not a smaller version of another role, it is an unenforced no-op, and the system must fail the invite flow (or route it into an existing modeled role) rather than mint an unenforceable identity.
WhyAn authorization model is not the union of every role name that appears in a column comment; it is the set of roles that have an actual, checkable predicate somewhere. A role that exists in the schema and in an onboarding flow but nowhere in the enforcement layer is worse than no role at all: it creates a false sense that a permission boundary exists ('staff have restricted access') when the real boundary is binary (dashboard reachable or not), and the eventual fix is discovered by a real staff member hitting a wall, not by anyone reading a spec.

high No gate checks object-level (IDOR/BOLA) authorization; the one authz-adjacent gate only checks that SOME auth call exists authz-rls-03
The rule to addA route that accepts a client-supplied object id (a path param or body field ending in _id, or a bare id, that is used in a WHERE/eq/match against a privileged table) must, in the same file, load that row and assert the caller's identity against an ownership or scope column (owner_id, user_id, salon_id via a join, staff_salon_id) before performing the privileged read or write. Passing an authentication check (a valid, logged-in getUser()) is necessary but never sufficient proof that this happened, and no gate should treat it as sufficient.
WhyOWASP's own API Security Top 10 has ranked Broken Object Level Authorization #1 in both its 2019 and 2023 editions specifically because this exact substitution, 'the user is logged in, therefore the request is authorized', is the most common real API bug: a role check answers a coarse question the code CAN get right while still leaking a horizontal check the code got wrong for one specific row. A codebase that only gates on 'is there an auth signal in this file' will pass code review and pass its own hook while shipping a route that updates any booking by id regardless of whose it is, because 'getUser() is present' says nothing about what happens after it.
Proof/Users/sulo/.claude/hooks/no-unauth-money-route.py is the only hook in the estate that inspects authorization shape on a new route, and its own docstring states its AUTH_SIGNALS list is deliberately just presence checks: 'auth.getUser(', 'requireAdmin(', 'CRON_SECRET', 'applyRateLimit', etc, with an explicit comment that a bare Supabase client was REMOVED from the signal list precisely because 'it must co-occur with an actual session read... to count' -- but the gate stops at session read, it never inspects whether the file also checks the object id against an ownership column. A route can satisfy this gate completely (calls getUser(), is logged in) while still doing `admin.from('bookings').update({...}).eq('id', bodyBookingId)` with zero ownership predicate, and nothing in this repo's tooling would flag it. Of 357 route.ts files, 236 call getUser() but only 96 reference owner_id anywhere in the file (a rough proxy, not a precise count, since many of those 96 overlaps are legitimately public-salon-lookup routes that read owner_id for display, not for a check) -- the gap between 236 and 96 is not itself proof of vulnerable routes, but it is proof that no tooling distinguishes 'authenticated' routes that also perform an object check from ones that don't.
Already therepartial: research/authz.md section 3 states the principle correctly and in detail (T1, OWASP API1:2023) and names the exact Solen instance already documented in _docs/BACKEND.md (the availability_slots/bookings RLS-client trap). What is missing is the enforcement half: the research recommends the rule but nothing checks that a NEW route actually follows it, and the one gate that touches this area (no-unauth-money-route.py) explicitly only checks for authentication presence, not the object check.

The rule to addEvery createAdminSupabaseClient() call site must have, in the same function, an explicit and visibly-commented ownership/role assertion immediately before the privileged query it protects, because BYPASSRLS means the database enforces nothing at all for that connection. A periodic (not one-time) sampling audit of a fixed fraction of call sites (for example 10% per quarter, or all NEW call sites added since the last audit) must confirm this holds, because the count only grows as the codebase grows and prose-only discipline decays under time pressure.
WhyThe service-role key maps to a Postgres role with the BYPASSRLS attribute, which is not a client-library setting that degrades gracefully, it is a hard database-level bypass evaluated per-connection regardless of what headers, comments, or intentions the calling code carries. Once a query runs on that connection, the database's own defense-in-depth layer (RLS, which this project's own research correctly calls its 'real enforcement layer') contributes nothing; the entire authorization decision for that call collapses onto whatever a human remembered to type in application code, and 270 independent, unaudited places for that memory to fail is a materially larger attack surface than every RLS policy gap combined, by the research's own reasoning.
Proofgrep -rl createAdminSupabaseClient app lib returns 270 files (this session's own count; research/authz.md's earlier count of 267 is close enough to confirm it is not shrinking). A quick heuristic sweep this session (files with createAdminSupabaseClient but no getUser()/owner_id/role check/CRON_SECRET/webhook-signature pattern anywhere in the same file) flagged 71 files; spot-checking two of them (app/api/bookings/[id]/dispute/route.ts, app/api/directory/[id]/claim/route.ts) showed the check is real but funneled through a shared helper (resolveBookingActor()) my grep pattern missed, so the true unchecked count is unknown, not zero and not 71 -- exactly the situation an unaudited surface produces: nobody, including this research pass, can currently state the real number with confidence.

RLS provides zero protection once you're on the service-role client'). What is missing is any verification that the invariant is actually followed, at any point in time, for any subset of the 270 sites.

medium Several tables carry unscoped WITH CHECK (true) INSERT policies that let a direct PostgREST caller bypass all app-layer business logic authz-rls-06
The rule to addAn INSERT policy on a table whose rows carry a salon_id, staff_id, or price/amount field must scope WITH CHECK to that identity (auth.uid() = user_id, or an EXISTS check against the owning salon/staff), never WITH CHECK (true), unless the table is genuinely intended to accept anonymous, unscoped writes (a newsletter signup, a public contact form) and that intent is stated in a comment on the policy itself.
WhyThe app's own API routes are not the only path to the database once a Supabase anon or authenticated key exists client-side; anyone can call PostgREST directly with that same key. An unscoped WITH CHECK (true) INSERT policy means every business rule the app enforces in TypeScript (a booking's price matches the service's real price, an inventory row belongs to the salon that owns it, a staff calendar entry belongs to the staff member who owns it) is opt-in for a legitimate client and completely absent for a client that skips the app and calls the database directly, which is a normal, unprivileged thing to do with a public anon key, not an exotic attack.
Proofgrep found FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true) (no scoping predicate) still live and never dropped on at least: bookings (001_booking_reviews.sql, 'Public can insert bookings'), salon_photos (004_salon_photos.sql, 'Authenticated users can insert salon photos'), addons (006_bleaching_addons.sql, 'Auth insert addons'), inventory (005_dashboard_upgrades.sql, 'Auth insert inventory'), sms_reminders and staff_calendars (005_dashboard_upgrades.sql), loyalty_stamps (039_loyalty.sql, 'loyalty_stamps_insert_system'), and quartier_subscriptions (064_quartier_subscriptions.sql). Some of these (quartier_subscriptions, a public newsletter-style signup) are legitimately unscoped by design; others (inventory, staff_calendars, addons) attach to a specific salon or staff member and have no predicate tying the inserted row's salon_id/staff_id to the caller at all, meaning any authenticated user (any customer with a normal login) can insert an inventory row, a staff calendar entry, or an addon definition under ANY salon's id via a direct PostgREST call.

medium RLS's silent-zero-rows failure mode has no enforcement in authorization-sensitive writes despite three confirmed prior incidents authz-rls-07
The rule to addEvery write (.update()/.delete()) against a privileged table, whether issued on the session client or the admin client, must check the actual number of affected rows (via .select() after the write, or checking the returned array length / count) and treat zero rows as an explicit failure path, never as an implicit success. This binds hardest on writes gated by RLS ownership predicates, because a zero-row result there is indistinguishable, from the response alone, between 'correctly refused an unauthorized caller' and 'silently failed to do the authorized thing.'
WhyPostgREST (and by extension Supabase's client libraries) returns error: null for an UPDATE/DELETE that matched zero rows, which is a database-correct response (no error occurred) but an application-dangerous one, because the two possible causes of zero rows, a bug and a security boundary working as intended, look byte-for-byte identical to code that only checks the error field. This is a generic Postgres/PostgREST fact, not a Solen quirk, but it is uniquely dangerous in authorization-sensitive paths because the outcome that would normally be user-visible (an error, a 403) is instead swallowed and the caller can proceed believing a write happened.
ProofThis exact class is already documented as having bitten Solen three times: availability_slots writes from a non-owner session client (slots_manage_owner policy, per _docs/BACKEND.md), bookings rollback deletes at app/api/bookings/route.ts:541,549,554 routing through the session client instead of the documented claimSlot() admin-client helper (flagged, unresolved, in _docs/BACKEND.md section 2), and a now-fixed instance on group_bookings (_plans/BOOKING_BACKEND_AUDIT.md:187, closed by two migrations). Three confirmed live incidents of the identical failure shape is a pattern, not a one-off bug.
Already therepartial: the CLAUDE.md project instructions already name this as the project's '#1 silent failure mode' in general (the Silent no-ops section) and research/authz.md's Myths and traps section restates it specifically for authorization writes. The gap is purely enforcement: it is repeated as advice in at least three places and has caused three confirmed incidents, which is precisely the 'advice gets outranked under task focus, a gate does not' pattern this project's own /harden methodology exists to fix, yet no such gate has been built for this specific, well-evidenced case.

medium No differentiated authorization tier exists for the owner/staff dashboard session versus a browsing customer session, despite its documented adjacency to Stripe Connect payouts authz-rls-08
The rule to addA session that can reach the salon-owner or staff dashboard (one hop from Stripe Connect payout control and from other customers' PII) must require re-authentication (a fresh password/MFA check, not just a valid existing session) before the highest-blast-radius actions specifically: changing the connected Stripe payout account, changing the account email/password, or granting a new staff invite. This is a stricter bar than 'is this session currently valid', and it is currently the same bar as a customer browsing salons.
WhyNot every authenticated session carries the same risk if compromised. A stolen customer session can see one person's bookings; a stolen salon-owner session sits adjacent to money movement (payouts) and other customers' contact data, so the cost of a false negative (an attacker with a stolen owner session doing real damage before anyone notices) is categorically higher, and the cost of a false positive (an owner having to re-enter a password once before changing bank details) is categorically lower than the cost to a customer of the same friction on every login. Treating all four roles as equally risky because they run through identical authentication code is optimizing for code simplicity over the actual blast-radius shape of the product.
Proofmiddleware.ts's dashboard gate (lines 148-224) checks role once per request and applies the identical session-validity bar to every dashboard route, from a staff calendar view to (if the feature existed) a payout-account change; there is no step-up/reauth call anywhere in app/api/dashboard/** or app/api/staff/** (grepped, zero hits for a password-confirmation or MFA-challenge pattern in any dashboard-adjacent route). Solen's own Stripe Connect payout wiring (app/api/tips/route.ts:142, app/api/walkin/tip/route.ts:160, per research/authz.md's own Stripe trap) already routes real money through stripeAccountId read off the salons row, so the adjacency this principle is about is not hypothetical, it's already live.

Neither research file states a reauth-on-sensitive-action rule as its own line item.

low FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is confirmed absent on every table, and the session-client's Postgres role identity has never been checked authz-rls-09
The rule to addVerify once, and record the answer as law rather than as an open question: which Postgres role does the Supabase 'authenticated'/'anon' session-client connection actually run as, and does that role own any table it's supposed to be RLS-restricted on. If (as is virtually certain for a standard Supabase project) the session client never runs as the table owner, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is moot for app traffic and the law should say so explicitly, closing the question instead of leaving it open indefinitely; if any operational script, migration runner, or reporting connection ever runs as the table owner against production data, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY must be set on every RLS-enabled table before that access pattern ships.
WhyPostgres's own documented default is that a table's OWNER role bypasses its own RLS policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is explicitly set; this is a genuinely surprising default (most people assume 'RLS enabled' means 'RLS always applies') and it is exactly the shape of silent-hole this whole file researches. Leaving it as an open, unverified question forever costs nothing until the day someone adds an operational script, a reporting connection, or a data-migration tool that happens to connect as the table owner, at which point every RLS policy in the project silently does nothing for that connection and nobody would know without already knowing to check this specific thing.
Proofgrep -rn 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' supabase/migrations -> zero hits across all 269+ migration files, confirming (this session, not just 'unverified' as research/authz.md left it) that no table in this project has ever had FORCE RLS applied. _inventory/_db-snapshot.json (capturedAt: 2026-07-12, 146 tables, rlsDisabled: []) confirms ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is universal, which is the weaker guarantee Postgres's own docs warn does not bind the owner role.

This finding upgrades the first half (is FORCE RLS set) from speculation to a confirmed grep result and leaves the second half (session-client role identity) exactly as open as before, since that requires a live database query this read-only research pass cannot run.

low The one admin-impersonation-shaped route writes no audit trail, despite an existing, used audit_log table and 26 other admin routes doing so authz-rls-10
The rule to addAny route that lets one identity act as, view as, or preview data scoped to another identity (an admin previewing a salon's dashboard, a future 'view as this customer' support tool) must write an audit_log row (actor id, target id/type, action name, timestamp) at the moment of that access, using the same logAuditEvent() helper every other privileged admin action in this codebase already uses, before the feature's scope is ever widened beyond a narrow, low-risk starting case.
WhyImpersonation is the one authorization pattern where 'the check passed' is not the end of the story: even a correctly role-gated, correctly scoped impersonation grants visibility into another party's data, and the only backstop against that capability being misused (not attacked, misused, by a legitimate admin acting outside their remit) is a durable, admin-visible-to-all record of who did it, to whom, when, and ideally why. A capability with no audit trail is a private backdoor even when its access control is otherwise perfect, because 'perfect access control' only proves the RIGHT PEOPLE can use it, not that they always should.
Proofapp/api/admin/preview-salon/route.ts is correctly role-gated (admin only) and correctly scoped (restricted to [TEST]%-prefixed salons only, a 1-hour cookie), but never calls lib/audit.ts's logAuditEvent(), the exact helper 26 other admin routes (salon approve/reject/freeze/warn, commission changes, feature-flag toggles, discovery moderation) already call for actions of comparable or lower sensitivity. Today this is low-risk specifically because the route is scoped to test salons only, meaning no real customer/salon data is exposed by it yet, but a support-tooling feature request to 'preview a REAL salon's dashboard to debug an issue' is a natural, likely next step, and it would inherit this same silent-audit-trail gap unless it's closed first.

It is filed under the authn audit rather than an authz one, which is a reasonable categorization (impersonation sits at the authn/authz boundary) but means it is easy to miss if a future session only reads authz.md and assumes impersonation is out of scope there.

high Cookie-authed multipart uploads have no CSRF defense input-abuse-01
The rule to addEvery route that accepts multipart/form-data and authenticates via the Supabase session cookie (createServerSupabaseClient() + auth.getUser()) must add an explicit CSRF defense before shipping: either require a custom header a plain HTML form cannot send (e.g. verify Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin, or a double-submit token), or switch the route to the same manually-attached Authorization: Bearer pattern app/api/salons/[slug]/gallery/route.ts already uses. A route is exempt from this rule ONLY if it is strictly JSON (Content-Type: application/json) or bearer-token-authenticated; the combination of multipart/form-data plus cookie auth is never exempt, no matter how small the surface looks.
WhyA cookie is attached automatically by the browser on a simple cross-site <form> POST (SameSite=Lax permits it on a top-level navigation), and multipart/form-data is a CORS-simple content type, so no preflight ever fires and the origin allowlist in middleware.ts is never consulted. An attacker's page can therefore silently trigger the write while the victim is merely logged into Solen in the same browser. This directly falsifies the project's own stated CSRF safety argument for exactly the routes that use this shape: security.md section 4 builds its whole 'Solen has no real CSRF surface' conclusion on every mutating route being JSON + CORS-allowlisted, and explicitly names multipart/form-data as the one shape that would silently defeat it -- treating that as a hypothetical future risk rather than checking whether it already exists.
Proof8 of the 9 app/api/**/route.ts files calling req.formData() authenticate via createServerSupabaseClient()+auth.getUser() (cookie-based, no header the browser wouldn't auto-send): app/api/clients/[id]/photos/route.ts:13-14, app/api/salon/documents/route.ts:9-10, app/api/profile/avatar/route.ts:38-39, app/api/services/[id]/photos/route.ts:14-15, app/api/reviews/[id]/photos/route.ts:14-15, app/api/dashboard/coiffeur/formula-photo/route.ts:13-14, app/api/admin/discovery/upload/route.ts:11-12, app/api/services/import/route.ts:10-11. Only app/api/salons/[slug]/gallery/route.ts:57 reads an Authorization: Bearer header a form cannot forge, and is therefore CSRF-safe by construction; the other 8 are not. Practical impact per route: forced upload of an attacker-chosen (but MIME-allowlisted) image onto a client's before/after photo record, a salon's verification document, a user's profile avatar, or a review's photo gallery, with the victim never seeing it happen.
Already therepartial: _backend-system/research/security.md section 4 correctly derives that JSON+CORS-allowlist protects Solen's JSON routes from CSRF, and explicitly names multipart/form-data as the one shape that would silently defeat that protection ('if a future route ever accepts multipart/form-data... this protection silently stops applying to that one route and nobody will notice until it's exploited'). It frames this as a future risk to watch for, not a present fact; it did not check whether any route already has this shape. _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md has no CSRF rule at all (S1-S6 cover auth/RLS/validation/secrets, none mention CSRF or form-based auth).

high Every upload route trusts client file.type; zero server-side magic-byte checks exist input-abuse-02
The rule to addEvery route that accepts a file upload verifies the file's real type by reading its first bytes and checking the format's magic-byte signature server-side (e.g. via the file-type package or an equivalent manual check), in addition to, never instead of, the client-declared file.type/extension allowlist, before the bytes are written to Storage or used to set the object's served Content-Type.

That fix closed the gap at the Storage-layer bucket config for that one bucket; the application-layer root cause (trusting file.type at all) is untouched and repeats identically in every other upload route today.

high Unescaped salon name in breadcrumb JSON-LD is a live stored-XSS vector input-abuse-03
The rule to addEvery dangerouslySetInnerHTML call that embeds JSON.stringify() of an object containing any DB-sourced or user-editable field goes through one shared, tested helper (e.g. safeJsonLdStringify()) that escapes '<' so a value containing '</script>' cannot terminate the script tag early. Raw JSON.stringify() is never passed directly into dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere in the codebase, including call sites whose data is 'currently' static, since a later edit can silently make it dynamic.
WhyJSON.stringify does not escape forward slashes, so a literal '</script>' inside a string value survives verbatim into the HTML source. The browser's HTML parser runs before JS parsing and closes the <script> tag on that literal text regardless of JS-string-escaping rules, letting anything that follows execute as raw markup -- the exact backend-caused XSS pattern OWASP's XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet names for JSON-LD-in-script blocks. This is not theoretical here: the fix already exists in this codebase, applied inconsistently.
Proofapp/[locale]/salon/[slug]/layout.tsx:128-138 builds a BreadcrumbList schema whose final item is { name: salon?.name ?? slug } -- salon.name is read straight from the salons table and is editable by the salon owner via the dashboard -- and renders it with dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(breadcrumb) }}, with zero escaping. The same page, one file over, app/[locale]/_components/salon/SalonDetailV3.tsx:177-182, DOES escape '<' before stringifying its own JSON-LD block, with an explicit code comment naming the '</script>' breakout it defends against ('a salon name containing "</script>" can't break out of the script tag'). The correct fix exists in the repo; it was simply never applied to the sibling call site rendering the identical field on the identical page.

The rule to addEvery server-side fetch() whose URL argument is not a compile-time string literal pointing at a fixed, hardcoded first-party or well-known vendor host is passed through assertSafeFetchUrl() (or an equivalent IP-range check) before the request fires, with no exception carved out for 'the URL came from our own database' or 'the URL came from a trusted third-party API's own response' -- both are still request-time data, not compile-time constants, and both have been the actual origin of a URL that reached the guarded code path in this codebase.

The next incident is a certainty on the current trajectory, not a hypothetical risk.

The rule to addSolen serves a Content-Security-Policy header (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only for one full deploy cycle first, then enforcing Content-Security-Policy) with an explicit script-src/style-src/img-src/connect-src domain allowlist covering at minimum Stripe.js, Google Maps, PostHog, and 'self', before any further work proceeds on the assumption that a missed-escaping bug has a second line of defense.

The rule to addEvery API route that returns a client error responds with exactly one JSON shape: { error: { code: SCREAMING_SNAKE_STRING, message: string } }, status set on the HTTP status line, never duplicated as a body-only 'success' flag. medium Every outbound third-party fetch() call inside an API route has zero timeout, independent of the AI-generation case already flagged api-contracts-06
The rule to addAny fetch() call to a third-party HTTP endpoint inside a route.ts file passes an explicit AbortSignal.timeout(N) (N chosen per call: a few seconds for a fast lookup like a transit-station query, longer for a genuinely slow provider), so a hung third-party service fails the request in a controlled, fast, named way instead of consuming the serverless function's entire wall-clock budget and returning the platform's generic timeout error.
WhyA route handler running on a serverless function has a hard wall-clock ceiling; a fetch with no timeout can hold that budget hostage until the PLATFORM kills it, at which point the caller gets an opaque 502/504 with none of Solen's own error-shape or logging discipline attached, and any other work the handler still had to do (writing a DB row, sending a notification) never happens either.
Proofgrep for outbound fetch("https://...") calls in app/api found exactly 8 call sites: app/api/bookings/resend-access/route.ts, app/api/bookings/[id]/dispute/route.ts, app/api/bookings/[id]/report/route.ts, app/api/bookings/[id]/escalate/route.ts, app/api/auth/verify-phone/send/route.ts, app/api/admin/nail/generate/route.ts, app/api/loyalty/award/route.ts, app/api/dashboard/barber-reminders/send/route.ts. Checking each individually for AbortController or AbortSignal.timeout: 0 of 8 have one.
Already therepartial: _backend-system/research/api-design.md section 9 and the audit's API-10 row both correctly flag the SAME underlying platform risk (Netlify function wall-clock limits) but scope it narrowly to AI-generation routes needing a 202+poll architecture. The delta this finding adds: four of the eight zero-timeout call sites (resend-access, dispute, report, escalate, barber-reminders) have nothing to do with AI generation or long-running jobs, they are simple notification/SMS/webhook-style outbound calls that should be FAST and don't need job/poll infrastructure at all, they just need a timeout guard, a much cheaper and more general fix than the 202+poll architecture the existing research scoped this problem to.

medium No request-body size limit exists anywhere in the API surface api-contracts-08
The rule to addAny route handler that calls request.json() on a body that could plausibly grow large (an array-accepting batch endpoint, a text/description field, a base64-encoded upload) enforces an explicit maximum, either via a zod .max()/.length() constraint on the parsed shape or a raw byte-length check on the request before parsing; the default assumption for a NEW route is a body under a few KB unless a documented reason requires more.
WhyNext.js App Router Route Handlers, unlike the old Pages API's bodyParser, impose no default size limit on `request.json()`; the only backstop today is whatever ceiling the hosting platform enforces on the whole request, not anything Solen's own code chooses or can reason about per endpoint. An endpoint with no size discipline is a resource-exhaustion vector: a single request with an oversized array or string can consume disproportionate memory/CPU parsing it before any business-logic validation even runs, on a serverless function billed and rate-limited per invocation.
ProofThe dashboard/batch endpoint already named in api-contracts-09's sibling finding (audit row API-09) is a concrete live example: app/api/dashboard/batch/route.ts:27-31 casts the parsed body's `requests` field directly to `BatchKey[]` with only an `Array.isArray` check, no length cap, before fanning it out into a `Promise.all` of Supabase queries.

The rule to addEvery 201 Created response sets a Location header pointing at the created resource's canonical GET URL (e.g. `/api/bookings/{id}`), even when the same data is also echoed in the body. A route that creates a resource with no addressable GET-by-id endpoint yet must either add one or explicitly note in a code comment why Location is omitted.
WhyRFC 9110 section 15.3.2 pairs 201 with the expectation that the client can locate the new resource; a client that wants to re-fetch, deep-link, or share a reference to the thing it just created has to fall back to guessing a URL shape from the body's id field, which only works if every client independently knows the same URL-construction convention, exactly the kind of implicit coupling a Location header exists to remove.

low No stated policy for which endpoints should set Cache-Control, so caching is each author's ad hoc, undocumented call api-contracts-09
The rule to addA route handler explicitly sets one of exactly two cache policies: `Cache-Control: private, no-store` for anything reading or returning user-specific, payment, or auth-adjacent data (the safe default for a new route), or a documented public/anonymous cache policy (max-age + stale-while-revalidate, matching the existing `ANON_CACHE_HEADERS` pattern) for genuinely public, non-personalized data like the salon search/list endpoints. No route ships with neither set.
WhyDeliberate caching is a real, already-used pattern (lib/salons/cache-headers.ts's `ANON_CACHE_HEADERS`) but it's applied to only 4 of 357 route files today with no written rule for when a NEW route should reach for it, and more importantly no explicit no-store default stated for the routes that must NEVER be cached. If a CDN or edge cache is ever added in front of Netlify (a plausible future performance step), an endpoint that happens to look cacheable by a generic heuristic (a GET with no obvious auth header) but actually returns per-user or payment-status data would silently leak across users unless every such route already declares its own explicit no-store today.

critical Cron-health check detects failed runs, not missing runs observability-1
The rule to addEvery cron-health check must distinguish 'ran and failed' from 'never ran.' Maintain an EXPECTED_CRON_NAMES map (name to its scheduled interval) and, in the daily digest (or a dedicated check), assert for each name that a cron_runs row exists within 2x its own interval; treat a missing row as a failure at the same severity as ok:false, not silence. Separately, wire one externally-hosted heartbeat (a free dead-man's-switch service, or an UptimeRobot-style ping) so a fully disabled or silently-broken GitHub Actions scheduler is itself detected, independent of anything running inside GitHub Actions.
WhyAbsence-of-evidence read as evidence-of-absence is this project's own named #1 failure class (the 'silent no-ops' rule in CLAUDE.md, there applied to DB filters); here it applies to the monitoring system itself. If GitHub Actions ever stops scheduling the workflow (or a YAML edit silently breaks the schedule trigger), zero cron_runs rows get written, and the daily digest's own query for 'ok=false in the last 24h' returns zero, reporting a false 'all clear' on the exact day everything actually stopped. Right-sized now: a query rewrite plus one owner-account signup for the external heartbeat, not a paging platform; revisit a fuller on-call/paging tier only once there is more than one person who could be woken.
Proofapp/api/cron/daily-digest/route.ts lines 93-118: the only cron-health query is `.from('cron_runs').select(...).eq('ok', false).gte('ran_at', twentyFourHoursAgo)`, which returns nothing (and renders '0 cron failures') if a cron simply never ran. 26 cron routes exist under app/api/cron (`find app/api/cron -name route.ts | wc -l` = 26), all scheduled purely by `.github/workflows/cron-jobs.yml`'s `schedule:` triggers, with no code anywhere checking for the presence of an expected run.

None of this catches the scheduler itself going silent.

This is a money-path blind spot, not a hypothetical: the project already tracks a near-identical rotation risk for Apple's login secret in memory, so secret rotation is a known recurring operational event here.

critical Self-service data export omits every salon-authored client record, including the most sensitive ones privacy-compliance-02
The rule to addGET /api/profile/export must return every table where a row is keyed to the requesting user as a data subject, not only tables the user themselves wrote to. Before shipping any change to this route, the exported-table list and the erasure `TABLES_CLEARED`/cascade list must be diffed against each other and against a live grep of `client_id UUID.*REFERENCES profiles(id)` / `customer_id UUID.*REFERENCES auth.users(id)`; any table present in one list and absent from the other is a bug, not a design choice, unless a comment names the reason.
WhyGDPR Art. 15 (right of access) and Art. 20 (data portability), and nFADP Art. 25 (right to information), entitle a data subject to see personal data an organization holds ABOUT them, not only data they entered themselves. A salon's consultation notes, allergy log, or treatment photos of a client are exactly this: personal data the salon (acting for or alongside Solen) generated about the customer. An export that silently skips these tables makes the self-service access right materially incomplete, which is the specific mechanism a real DSAR complaint would test first.
Proofapp/api/profile/export/route.ts:20-142 lists exactly 18 tables via `.eq("user_id", user.id)` calls: profiles, salons (owned), bookings+booking_services, reviews, favorites, user_credits, credit_redemptions, notifications, notification_preferences, user_preferences, loyalty_status, referrals, discovery_saves, discovery_collections, discovery_comments, recurring_booking_rules, push_subscriptions, voucher_redemptions, tips. Cross-referencing the 69-table PII sweep of _inventory/_db-columns.json against this list, at least 13 tables holding first-party client data about the same user are absent from export: client_notes, consultation_notes, client_formulas, nail_client_preferences, hand_chart_notes, barber_cut_history, client_photos, spa_treatment_outcomes, waxing_sensitivity_log, wellness_journals, makeup_face_charts, bridal_workflows, fade_blueprints. All of these DO appear as delete/anonymize targets in app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts's TABLES_CLEARED array or cascade via a `client_id ... REFERENCES profiles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` FK (confirmed by reading the four dashboard-notes migrations directly), so Solen already treats them as the user's personal data for erasure purposes but not for access purposes.
Already therenone: this specific asymmetry between the export list and the erasure list is not named anywhere in _docs/BACKEND.md section 13 (which documents the export endpoint's 18 tables as a fact, not as a gap against the erasure list) or in security.md's Unverified section.

The rule to addAny column that reveals health status (allergy_notes, skin_sensitivity, medications, skin_condition, pain_level, skin_before/after) or is capable of revealing racial/ethnic origin (disc_skin_tone) must be behind an explicit, separately-recorded consent event distinct from general account creation or ToS acceptance, per GDPR Art. 9(2)(a) and nFADP Art. 6(2)/Art. 5(c). General 'necessary for performance of a contract' (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b)) is NOT a valid basis for Art. 9 special-category data on its own; explicit consent (or a narrow Art. 9(2) exemption Solen would need to name) is required regardless of whether the customer also agreed to book a service.
WhyA beauty/wellness booking product legitimately needs to know a client is allergic to a product or has sensitive skin, that's a real safety need, not a design mistake. But collecting it is legally a different, higher-obligation category of processing than 'what's your name and phone number,' and treating it identically means Solen has no record it ever obtained the specific consent this category of data requires, which is the first thing a regulator or a complainant checks.

high Third-party processors and the audit log are outside the erasure cascade, and the codebase already says so privacy-compliance-06
The rule to addEvery processor named in the privacy policy's own table that stores a copy of a user's PII (today: Stripe, PostHog) must have an erasure/anonymization call wired into app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts before a deletion run is considered complete for that user, OR the privacy policy must explicitly disclose the exception and its legal basis (e.g. Stripe's own 10-year financial-recordkeeping obligation as a controller in its own right). Additionally, `audit_log.metadata` jsonb payloads that carry a plaintext email (`{ email: user.email }`) must be scrubbed or hashed as part of the same erasure run, not left indefinitely because the FK-level `actor_id SET NULL` gives a false impression of completeness.
WhyAnonymize-not-delete only satisfies 'right to erasure' if it actually reaches every place the PII was copied to. A trigger that correctly nulls `bookings.guest_email` while a live Stripe Customer object and a PostHog person profile keep the same email under the same permanent user id is erasure in the primary database only, which is a materially different (and weaker) claim than what the product's own deletion UI implies to the user ('DELETE MY ACCOUNT').
Proof_docs/BACKEND.md section 13's own Gotchas paragraph states this outright: 'Stripe and PostHog are not part of the erasure cascade... This is a real gap against a strict right-to-erasure reading, not just a documentation nuance,' and separately: '`audit_log.metadata` can carry the erased user's email indefinitely... the metadata jsonb payload with the plaintext email is never scrubbed by the trigger, the cron, or any job found in this repo.' Verified live: `grep -rn "stripe.customers.del\|stripe.customers.delete" app lib` (per BACKEND.md's own cited grep) returns nothing; `identifyServerUser` in lib/posthog-server.ts sends the email as a person property with no corresponding delete call in the erasure cron.

medium No retention schedule exists; three independently-decided numbers stand in for one privacy-compliance-07
The rule to addEvery table holding personal data needs an explicit retention rule, stated as either a fixed duration, an event-triggered deletion (e.g. 'N days after the booking relationship ends'), or 'retained until account deletion, no independent limit,' with the reasoning named. A table with no stated rule defaults to 'retained until account deletion,' never to silent indefinite growth.
WhyGDPR Art. 5(1)(e) (storage limitation) and the equivalent nFADP proportionality principle both require that retention be actively justified, not merely 'whatever happens by default.' Right now Solen has three retention numbers that were each decided for a different reason (financial law, a 2026-07-10 OTP-logging sweep, an ad hoc 90-day search-anonymization job) and calls that 'data retention' in its own runbook, while several tables holding real personal or health-adjacent data have never had the question asked.

medium Whether a salon is a controller, joint controller, or processor for the notes it writes is never decided privacy-compliance-09
The rule to addFor every table where a salon (not Solen) originates the personal data (client_notes, consultation_notes, and the category-specific note/photo tables), name explicitly whether the salon is acting as an independent controller, a joint controller with Solen, or a processor acting on Solen's instructions, because this determines who owes the data subject which right, and whether a controller-to-controller (or joint-controller Art. 26 GDPR / equivalent nFADP) agreement is needed between Solen and each of its 28 salon partners.

If that's correct, the salon (not just Solen) independently owes that client the GDPR/nFADP data-subject rights for that data, and Solen's platform-wide erasure/export mechanisms are doing the salon's compliance work without an agreement that says so.

low GDPR applies only if Solen actually targets EU data subjects; that determination is never made explicit and the policy currently hedges rather than deciding privacy-compliance-12
The rule to addState explicitly, once, which regime is primary: Solen is a Swiss sole proprietorship serving (per its own domain and the seeded salon set) Swiss customers, so nFADP is the primary and binding regime under Swiss law regardless of language. GDPR only attaches extraterritorially under Art. 3(2) if Solen actively offers services to, or monitors the behavior of, individuals physically in the EU (e.g. targeted marketing in euros, EU-specific delivery/service availability), not merely because the site is available in French/Italian or a tourist from the EU happens to book a Swiss salon while visiting. Until that determination is made and documented, don't build EU-specific machinery (a full RoPA, an EU representative under Art. 27 GDPR) reflexively, and don't tell users 'you have GDPR rights' if Solen has not concluded GDPR actually applies to them.

9
high Lint/type debt is a global ratchet, never diff-scoped, never required to shrink fe-01
The rule to addEvery PR's lint and type check runs twice: once as the existing repo-wide ratchet (must not exceed the current baseline), and once scoped ONLY to lines changed in that PR (via git diff against the merge-base), where the changed-lines pass must be zero-error for @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any, no-unused-vars, and no-html-link-for-pages, with no baseline exception. Separately, the repo-wide lint baseline (currently frozen at 481 since the gate was created) is lowered by a fixed amount on a fixed cadence (for example 20 errors per calendar month) until it reaches 0; a month where it does not move is logged as its own entry in _tasks/INCOMPLETE_FEATURES.md.
WhyA global ratchet only guarantees the total count never goes up. It does not guarantee that NEW code is clean, because a PR can add 5 new `any`s in file A while an unrelated PR removes 5 in file B, and both individually pass. That laundering is exactly why the baseline has not moved since it was set. Without a diff-scoped floor, 'any' discipline exists only on paper: the rule is already configured as an ESLint ERROR (verified below), so the gap is not the rule text, it is that nothing stops the count from staying frozen forever.
Proofnext.config.mjs:9 sets eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds:true (lint never blocks a production build) while typescript.ignoreBuildErrors:false (type errors do). .github/workflows/quality.yml's lint job compares npm run lint output against BASELINE=481 and only fails if the count goes UP; git log -p shows this baseline was set once (commit ed5cf0557) and never lowered since, while the sibling tsc ratchet in the same file WAS driven from BASELINE=5 to BASELINE=0 in a later commit (53c1890ea) -- proving the team can do a real paydown when it decides to, it just never scheduled one for lint. A live `npm run lint` run (1209 output lines) breaks down as: 354 @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any (classified as Error), 64 no-html-link-for-pages (Error -- real internal <a> tags to /privacy/, /datenschutz/, / that force full page reloads instead of Next.js client navigation), 55 no-unescaped-entities (Error), 210 @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars (Warning), 16 no-img-element (Warning, bypasses next/image). Separately, `as any` appears 338 times and bare `!.` non-null assertions ~31 times across app/components/lib. No husky, lint-staged, or .git/hooks/pre-commit exists, and no .claude hook targets `any` or unused-var introduction at write time.

high No state-ownership doctrine (URL vs server props vs Context vs local); the tree is 37% client-rendered with 171 files fetching client-side fe-03
The rule to addState picks exactly one owner, in this priority order: (1) anything that should be shareable, back-button-safe, or survive a refresh (a filter, an active tab, a search query, a selected date) lives in the URL via searchParams, never in component state; (2) anything known at request time and not re-computed per-interaction is fetched once in the nearest Server Component and passed down as a prop, never re-fetched client-side with useEffect; (3) anything shared by more than two sibling client components on one page lives in a single page-scoped Context/reducer (the existing BookingProvider pattern), never duplicated per component; (4) everything else is local useState. A new client component that calls fetch() inside useEffect for data that was already available on the server at request time is a violation unless the file states why (e.g. it genuinely depends on a client-only value like geolocation or a just-completed client action).
WhyWithout a stated ownership order, each new surface re-derives the same fetch/loading/error boilerplate independently (171 separate implementations), duplicates the same data across sibling components instead of sharing one fetch, and drifts further client-side over time because nothing tells a new agent that server-fetch-then-pass-as-props is the default, not the exception, this is a Next.js App Router product.
Proof296 of 799 .ts/.tsx files under app/ contain "use client" (37%); 175 of 197 files under components/+components-legacy/ do too. 171 files combine useEffect with fetch( for client-side data loading, against a total of only 190 files that call fetch( anywhere -- i.e. almost every fetch call in the whole tree is a client-side one, not a server-fetched prop. This directly contradicts the project's own Rule 42 template (_rules/STRUCTURAL_RULES.md) which states new feature pages should have 'app/[locale]/[feature]/page.tsx <- Server Component (data fetching)' feeding a client component for interactivity only -- a pattern the salon PDP and booking-wizard shell DO follow (_docs/FRONTEND.md documents both as RSC-fetch-then-pass-props) but which is evidently the minority pattern once you count the whole tree.
Already therepartial: Rule 42's file-tree template implies server-fetch-then-client-render for new pages, and the booking flow's BookingProvider is a real, working example of page-scoped Context for shared state. Neither is generalized into a rule that a new PR can be graded against, and there is no URL-vs-Context-vs-local decision tree anywhere.

critical Legally and financially significant transactional emails accept a locale argument and silently ignore it, always sending German seo-comms-04
The rule to addA template function's signature must not lie: if a function accepts a `locale: EmailLocale` parameter, its subject and body must branch on that parameter in every code path; a template with a locale parameter that has no effect on output is worse than one with no parameter at all, because every caller reasonably assumes localization is happening.
WhyA no-show charge, a late-cancellation fee, a refund, an upcharge, or an account suspension are financially or legally consequential notices; sending them only in German to a customer whose stored profile.locale is fr, it or en means that customer cannot understand why they were charged or suspended, which is both a support-ticket generator and, for the fee/charge emails specifically, arguably inadequate notice for a contested charge.
Prooflib/email-templates/audit-notifications.ts defines 19 functions (bookingPendingApprovalEmail through salonStrikeEmail, lines 3-147), every one typed `locale: EmailLocale = "de"` in its signature, and every one's subject/html string is hardcoded German with zero reference to the `locale` variable anywhere in the function body (confirmed by reading all 148 lines; `de=0 en=0 fr=0 it=0` locale-branch markers found by grep, versus lib/email.ts's 55-61 per-language markers in the properly localized templates). This is not dead code: lib/bookings/notify-no-show-fee.ts line 73 and lib/bookings/notify-refund.ts line 80 both correctly fetch `profile.locale` from the database and pass the real user locale into noShowChargeEmail/refundProcessedEmail, so a French-speaking customer's actual locale is threaded all the way to the template call and then dropped on the floor inside the template itself.

low No bounce, complaint, or suppression handling exists for outbound email; nothing stops re-sending to a dead or complaining address seo-comms-10
The rule to addOnce real send volume exists, a webhook from the email provider (Resend) must record bounce and complaint events into a suppression table, and sendEmail must check that table before every send; until that volume exists, this is correctly deferred, not correctly absent forever.
WhyRepeated sends to a hard-bouncing or complaining address are the primary mechanism by which a sending domain's reputation degrades at providers like Gmail and Outlook; once reputation degrades, transactional mail (booking confirmations, payment receipts) starts landing in spam for everyone, not just the bad addresses, which is a much worse failure than the missing feature itself.

low Bare-path locale redirect uses Accept-Language + cookie with no documented, stable default-locale policy for crawlers seo-comms-12
The rule to addThe locale a crawler or first-time visitor with no cookie is redirected to from a bare path (e.g. solen.ch/salon/foo) must be a single, documented, stable default (this project's default is 'de' per i18n.ts), and that default must be what x-default in hreflang alternates points to; Accept-Language-based redirects are acceptable for human visitors but must never be the value search engines see, since crawler Accept-Language behavior is inconsistent and unversioned by Google itself.

high Confidence-tiering is claim-shape-gated, not a blanket rule agent-output-1
The rule to addEvery load-bearing claim in a final reply (a state-of-the-world statement the owner will act on: 'this works', 'this covers all 28 salons', 'this is safe to ship', 'this pattern affects N files') is tagged verified, expect, or assume before the reply ends. The tag is required regardless of whether the sentence happens to contain one of the specific trigger words (fixed/done/verified/confirmed/resolved) that today's gates scan for.
WhyRule 15 defines the three-tier system (verified/expect/assume) but its trigger is narrow: 'a claim that can be checked against the live world', mainly versioned/external facts. The actual enforcement is five separate narrow regex gates, each covering one claim SHAPE: verify-before-done-gate only fires on the literal words fixed/done/fertig/erledigt/verified/confirmed/resolved/works now/passes; stat-source-gate only fires on persuasion-statistic shapes (n% of users, studies show, Nx more); paint-proof-gate only fires on visibility/occlusion claims about fixed/sticky/overlay elements; env-claim-needs-evidence-gate only fires on sandbox/permission-block claims; checkbox-evidence-gate only fires on a newly ticked `- [x]` line. A load-bearing claim outside these five shapes (e.g. 'this query is safe for concurrent bookings', 'the migration is backward compatible', 'this covers every route') carries no confidence tag requirement and no gate.

The rule system itself

12
critical A gate skip-flagged past a set rate must be re-scoped or retired, not left as a live-but-ignored law gate-mute-forces-rescope
The rule to addAny gate whose skip-flag fires more than 10 times in a rolling 7 days (or more than 3 times for a single-purpose gate that is not a shared family) is automatically flagged at the next SessionStart as REQUIRES-DECISION: the owner picks narrow-scope, merge-into-family, or retire within 7 days, and until that decision is made the gate's deny message states out loud that it is under review. A gate that keeps firing and keeps getting skipped is not enforcing anything; it is a toll the owner pays to keep working, and the system currently has no mechanism that turns that toll into a forcing question.
WhyLAW_SYSTEM.md section 2 says a misfiring gate must be TUNED, never silently disabled, because 'a disabled gate is a lie: everyone believes the law is enforced and nobody is enforcing it.' But a gate that is skip-flagged 72 times in 6 days is functionally disabled by a thousand tiny cuts instead of one big one, and the same lie results: system-health-check.py reports it as wired and enforcing, when in practice it enforces almost nothing. Nothing currently distinguishes 'skipped twice for real exceptions' from 'skipped every single time it fires.'
Proof_plans/SELF_AUDIT_2026-07-25.md section 2: the 7-member mockup gate family was skip-flagged 72 times in 6 days (28+14+13+9+8+4+4+... across mockup-approved/preflight/content/lang-icon/grounding/real-base/english); finish-autonomously-skip.flag alone was used 40 times in 6 days, 'the single most-muted gate.' Both are explicitly logged as 'OWNER CALL, parked' with no automatic trigger -- the audit had to notice this by hand-reading a 745-line log, and next week's self-audit will have to notice it by hand again.

critical No test that a new law/gate/doctrine layer must be provably cheaper than the mistakes it prevents before it is written law-layer-roi-test
The rule to addBefore authoring a new doctrine file, gate family, or research-to-law layer (the shape _backend-system's research/ folder is currently in, 15 files with no LAW.md yet), the proposal must name: (a) the specific, counted incidents it would have prevented in the last 90 days, (b) the ongoing per-session cost it adds (injection bytes, extra tool calls, extra doc a human must read), and (c) a one-line comparison showing (a) outweighs (b).
